item.title: BEYOND on Tour V: Redefining Rest, Recovery and the Future of African Wellness
item.description: From its signature Sunset Ride at Lakowe Lakes to personalised recovery experiences and dermatological skincare innovation, BEYOND Fitness Africa is creating a new expression of wellness rooted in movement, culture and community. African wellness is evolving, and BEYOND Fitness Africa is helping shape what comes next. From 30 October to 1 November 2026, BEYOND Fitness Africa returns to Lakowe Lakes Golf and Country Resort for the fifth edition of BEYOUND on Tour , its signature destination wellness retreat. Built around the theme Rest, Reset and Recover , the three-day experience invites guests to step away from everyday demands and reconnect with their wellbeing through movement, personalised recovery, nourishing food, meaningful connections and genuine rest. This year’s edition features an expanded partnership with La Roche-Posay, the Official Dermatological Skincare Partner, connecting the retreat’s approach to wellbeing with expert skincare education and the brand’s upcoming Living Lab experience in Lagos. From Lagos to a Broader African Wellness Vision Founded in 2021, BEYOND Fitness Africa has spent five years building a premium community around high-performance group fitness, recovery and human connection. What began as a boutique fitness studio in Victoria Island has evolved into a wellness business spanning corporate wellness, destination retreats and brand collaborations, with ambitions to expand beyond Lagos into other Nigerian and African markets. BEYOND on Tour has become an important expression of that vision. Its fourth edition captured widespread attention when guests cycled beside the lake at sunset while Loud Urban Choir performed live, creating an unforgettable fusion of movement, music and nature. The fifth edition builds on that momentum, offering a more expansive recovery programme and greater freedom for guests to experience the weekend on their own terms. Simisola Williams, Founder and Managing Director of BEYOND Fitness Africa, explains: “When I founded BEYOND, I wanted to create a space where people could invest in their wellbeing while continuing to pursue full, ambitious lives. “Five years on, that vision has grown beyond our Victoria Island studio. Through BEYOND on Tour, we’re creating opportunities for people to step away from their routines and experience wellness differently. “What we’ve learnt is that people need different things at different moments. Sometimes it’s movement and the energy of a community. Other times, it’s rest, recovery or simply the freedom to do nothing. “As we look towards expanding BEYOND beyond Lagos, our ambition is to build a distinctly African wellness brand that delivers exceptional experiences while helping people live healthier, fuller lives.” Three Days of Movement, Recovery and Connection BEYOND on Tour V offers an all-inclusive retreat where guests can shape their weekend around what they need most. From Lagos to a Broader African Wellness Vision Founded in 2021, BEYOND Fitness Africa has spent five years building a premium community around high-performance group fitness, recovery and human connection. What began as a boutique fitness studio in Victoria Island has evolved into a wellness business spanning corporate wellness, destination retreats and brand collaborations, with ambitions to expand beyond Lagos into other Nigerian and African markets. BEYOND on Tour has become an important expression of that vision. Its fourth edition captured widespread attention when guests cycled beside the lake at sunset while Loud Urban Choir performed live, creating an unforgettable fusion of movement, music and nature. The fifth edition builds on that momentum, offering a more expansive recovery programme and greater freedom for guests to experience the weekend on their own terms. Simisola Williams, Founder and Managing Director of BEYOND Fitness Africa, explains: “When I founded BEYOND, I wanted to create a space where people could invest in their wellbeing while continuing to pursue full, ambitious lives. “Five years on, that vision has grown beyond our Victoria Island studio. Through BEYOND on Tour, we’re creating opportunities for people to step away from their routines and experience wellness differently. “What we’ve learnt is that people need different things at different moments. Sometimes it’s movement and the energy of a community. Other times, it’s rest, recovery or simply the freedom to do nothing. “As we look towards expanding BEYOND beyond Lagos, our ambition is to build a distinctly African wellness brand that delivers exceptional experiences while helping people live healthier, fuller lives.” Three Days of Movement, Recovery and Connection BEYOND on Tour V offers an all-inclusive retreat where guests can shape their weekend around what they need most. The experience includes personalised IV infusions, full-body massages, assisted stretching, breathwork, recovery treatments and specialist wellness consultations, alongside thoughtfully curated dining and entertainment. Movement enthusiasts can enjoy Sunrise Sculpt, Aqua Conditioning, golf, mobility and Total Body Strength with adidas OG Sport. Aquafina, the Official Hydration Partner, supports guests throughout the programme. Beyond physical wellbeing, Mrs Ifeoma Monye will lead Pretty Balancing Act: Creating a Life System That Works , an insightful conversation on creating practical systems that support personal wellbeing, professional ambitions and the demands of everyday life. A highlight of the weekend is the return of the signature Sunset Ride, featuring a live performance by Loud Urban Choir beside the lake. Guests can also enjoy the performance from La Roche-Posay’s Sunset Viewing Lounge. The evening continues with Filmhouse After Dark, featuring karaoke, barbecue and cinema under the stars. BYD joins as Official Mobility Partner, while Instax, the Official Memory Partner, captures moments from the weekend. Together, these experiences bring BEYOND’s approach to movement, restoration and community to life. La Roche-Posay Brings Skin Health into the Wellness Experience As Official Dermatological Skincare Partner, La Roche-Posay will introduce a dedicated Skin Studio, offering guests one-to-one dermatologist consultations, personalised skincare education and practical sun protection guidance. The brand will also present Sunrise Sculpt, integrating skin health awareness into outdoor movement. For Williams, the collaboration reflects the importance of looking at wellbeing more holistically. “Wellbeing goes beyond exercise. It’s about understanding how different aspects of our health work together. Our partnership with La Roche-Posay brings skin health into that conversation, giving guests access to specialist knowledge they can apply in their everyday lives.” Beyond the Retreat: La Roche-Posay Living Lab Opens in Lagos Just days after BEYOND on Tour V, La Roche-Posay will bring its Living Lab to Victoria Island, Lagos, on 5 and 6 November 2026. The immersive public experience will bring together scientists, dermatologists, patients and consumers to explore skincare innovation and encourage meaningful conversations around skin health. Visitors will journey through five interactive stages: Discover, Test, Experience, Learn and Consult. The experience will feature Innovation Corners dedicated to La Roche-Posay’s Effaclar, Anthelios, Mela B3, Cicaplast and Lipikar ranges, alongside the LRP Café, expert discussions, the Scars of Life Cinema and professional skincare consultations. Designed to make dermatological science more accessible, Living Lab places real-life experiences and individual needs at the centre of skincare education and innovation. The event will take place at Plots 8 and 9, Ligali Ayorinde Street, beside GAC Motors, Victoria Island, Lagos, from 9 am to 7 pm on both days. Visitors can reserve their places at www.livinglabnigeria.com Building the Future of African Wellness For BEYOND Fitness Africa, its fifth destination retreat represents another step towards building a wellness brand with relevance and reach beyond Lagos. By combining premium fitness and recovery experiences with African music, culture, hospitality and specialist partnerships, BEYOND is demonstrating the potential for world-class wellness experiences created on the continent. As Williams puts it: “Africa has an incredible opportunity to shape the future of wellness. We have the creativity, talent, culture and a growing audience that understands the importance of investing in their wellbeing. Our ambition is to continue raising the standard of wellness experiences here while building a brand that helps people feel, function and live better.” As BEYOND on Tour enters its fifth edition, its message is simple: wellness is not only about how far we can push ourselves, but also about how intentionally we recover and care for ourselves along the way. item.description: As SpaceX impacts Ukraine and AI-generated music divides artists and fans, critics are asking what happens when technology has too much control over our lives This was originally published in TechScape, a newsletter about how technology shapes our lives. item.title: Labor and the Coalition are poised to take a reckless gamble on AI. Haven’t they realised community support has collapsed? | Edward Santow and Sarah Sacher
item.description: Australian workers expect the government to act to protect them from AI harms. There is a clear reform solution at hand Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast Australia’s major political parties are edging towards rare consensus. Labor and the Coalition increasingly want to take a major bet on artificial intelligence. Yet, just as the parties are coming together, the Australian community is running the other way. Last year, only 30% of Australians believed the benefits of AI outweighed the risks. In 2026, community trust in AI appears to be falling even further. Continue reading...

item.title: Red light, white light: How to preserve your night vision while using stargazing apps
item.description: The best stargazing apps can take your observation of the night sky to the next level, whether that's using augmented reality (AR mode) to identify stars or looking up the next lunar eclipse . However, the bright light emitted by smartphone screens can prevent your eyes from adjusting to the dark. If you're using one of the best telescopes , you'll want to preserve your night vision even more. Fortunately, there are ways to all but eliminate this problem. Why are bright screens bad for stargazing? The brighter your screen, the harder you'll find it to spot distant objects in the night sky. (Image credit: Getty Images) When you step out into the dark, it can take up to 20-30 minutes for your vision to adjust. The rod cells in your eyes build up a chemical known as rhodopsin, which gives you night vision. However, bright light bleaches that chemical, negatively impacting your night vision. So when you look through a telescope, binoculars or just turn your eyes to the night sky after peering at a bright phone screen, it'll be harder for you to pick out fainter objects such as galaxies and nebulas. One way of fixing this problem is simply to put your phone away and wait another 20-30 minutes. But if you're using a stargazing app to help you navigate the night skies, that's not really an option. The good news is that, between individual stargazing apps and your phone's own built-in features, you can minimize the impact of your smartphone's screen light. How to block white light in stargazing apps SkyView and several other stargazing apps let you apply a red filter. (Image credit: Skyview) Many of the best stargazing apps will let you enable a red light filter or similar, though this option may not always be present in the free version. Here's how to do that in three of our favorite stargazing apps: SkyView : Tap the screen, tap the horizontal lines, tap on Settings, then Display, then Night Mode and Red. Star Walk 2 : Tap the horizontal lines, tap on Settings, then tap the button next to Night Mode. Sky Tonight: Tap the horizontal lines, tap on Settings, then Tools, then Night Mode. All these modes will minimize the amount of white light coming from the app. However, be aware that this is only within the app. Once you go back to your phone's main menu, it will be at full color. With the red screen naturally looking darker, you may have turned up the brightness on your phone, so making the switch away from the app will be quite the shock. If you want to dim your whole phone or put it into red light mode, here's how to do that on Android or iPhone . How to block white light on Android phones Many Android phones, including recent Pixel and Samsung models, include the equivalent of a red filter. (Image credit: Samsung) On Android, there are several ways to minimize the impact of bright light, depending on the model and make of phone you have. item.dc:creator: Chris McMullen
item.content:encoded: The best stargazing apps can take your observation of the night sky to the next level, whether that's using augmented reality (AR mode) to identify stars or looking up the next lunar eclipse . However, the bright light emitted by smartphone screens can prevent your eyes from adjusting to the dark. If you're using one of the best telescopes , you'll want to preserve your night vision even more. Fortunately, there are ways to all but eliminate this problem. Why are bright screens bad for stargazing? The brighter your screen, the harder you'll find it to spot distant objects in the night sky. (Image credit: Getty Images) When you step out into the dark, it can take up to 20-30 minutes for your vision to adjust. The rod cells in your eyes build up a chemical known as rhodopsin, which gives you night vision. However, bright light bleaches that chemical, negatively impacting your night vision. So when you look through a telescope, binoculars or just turn your eyes to the night sky after peering at a bright phone screen, it'll be harder for you to pick out fainter objects such as galaxies and nebulas. One way of fixing this problem is simply to put your phone away and wait another 20-30 minutes. But if you're using a stargazing app to help you navigate the night skies, that's not really an option. The good news is that, between individual stargazing apps and your phone's own built-in features, you can minimize the impact of your smartphone's screen light. How to block white light in stargazing apps SkyView and several other stargazing apps let you apply a red filter. (Image credit: Skyview) Many of the best stargazing apps will let you enable a red light filter or similar, though this option may not always be present in the free version. Here's how to do that in three of our favorite stargazing apps: SkyView : Tap the screen, tap the horizontal lines, tap on Settings, then Display, then Night Mode and Red. Star Walk 2 : Tap the horizontal lines, tap on Settings, then tap the button next to Night Mode. Sky Tonight: Tap the horizontal lines, tap on Settings, then Tools, then Night Mode. All these modes will minimize the amount of white light coming from the app. However, be aware that this is only within the app. Once you go back to your phone's main menu, it will be at full color. With the red screen naturally looking darker, you may have turned up the brightness on your phone, so making the switch away from the app will be quite the shock. If you want to dim your whole phone or put it into red light mode, here's how to do that on Android or iPhone . How to block white light on Android phones Many Android phones, including recent Pixel and Samsung models, include the equivalent of a red filter. (Image credit: Samsung) On Android, there are several ways to minimize the impact of bright light, depending on the model and make of phone you have. One near-universal option is to dim your smartphone. Swipe down the notification panel from the top of the screen and you'll see a brightness slider. Slide this to the left to dim your phone. We'd also recommend disabling adaptive brightness in the Display section of your phone's settings. You may also have an Extra Dim option in the Accessibility menu — just don't dim the screen to the point of not being able to see it at all! Some Android phones, such as recent Samsung and Google Pixel models, also offer a Red Filter. On some, you'll find this in Accessibility, then Vision Enhancements, then Color Filter. You can then choose the color you want and also tweak the opacity. All the above options will let you continue to use your smartphone for stargazing, while minimizing its negative impact on your night vision. How to block white light on Apple iPhones Apple's iPhones also offer an option to minimize the effect of white light. (Image credit: Apple) As with Android phones, iPhones have a built-in option to dim the screen brightness. In this case, you swipe down from the top of the screen and look for the vertical brightness slider, represented by a sun icon. Reduce the slider as much as you're comfortable with, dimming the screen while still keeping it visible. Beyond that, recent iPhones also offer the ability to apply a color filter, again via their Accessibility options. Here's how to do that. First, tap on the Settings icon, then pick Accessibility. Select Display & Text Size and go to Color Filters. Tap the Color Filter button. Then, pick Color Tint and move the Hue and Intensity sliders all the way to the right. item.title: The view from the edge of a sparkling spiral galaxy | Space photo of the day for Oct. 20, 2026
item.description: null The spiral galaxy NGC 1827, as seen from the side by the Hubble Space Telescope. (Image credit: NASA, ESA, Michael Jones (California Institute of Technology); Image Processing: Gladys Kober (NASA/Catholic University of America)) If you were approaching the edge of a spiral galaxy, arriving from afar through the cosmos, it might look something like this. What is it? In this new snapshot by the Hubble Space Telescope 's Advanced Camera for Surveys (ACS), we can see the edge of the spiral galaxy NGC 1827. Found about 37 million light-years from Earth, this galaxy sparkles in this side-on view. Not all spiral galaxies are the same. This galaxy is what is known as an "intermediate" spiral, which means that its structure sits somewhere between that of a barred and unbarred spiral galaxy. Barred galaxies have a distinctive central, bar-shaped structure, while the unbarred variety lacks this bar and can look more like circular spirals. NGC 1827's spiral shape isn't clear from the side, however. From this perspective, we see its twinkling edge, speckled with stars and woven together with brown ribbons of dust. Why is it incredible? Beneath the beauty of this spiral edge lies an expansive, cosmic landscape. Bright blue stars dot the spiral's side, with one particularly luminous star taking the spotlight with four diffraction spikes — created by light bending through the inner workings of Hubble's camera — emanating from its center. This image was captured as part of a larger Hubble survey that's exploring 260 satellite galaxies, which are galaxies gravitationally bound to larger hosts. Hubble is specifically looking to survey satellite galaxies that lie near host galaxies similar to our own Milky Way . So far, Hubble has spotted 111 such satellites and will continue to observe, hunting for the rest. By studying satellite galaxies like this one, which also happens to be an especially low-mass galaxy, researchers could better understand the complicated dynamics both within the galaxies themselves and between them and their host galaxies.

item.title: HPE to launch AI straight to the Moon
item.description: Forget space datacenters. Before the end of the year, HPE will have AI running on the Moon. This isn’t some exec’s loony fantasy either. HPE has been building orbital compute platforms for the International Space Station (ISS) for years. Now, it’s sending its fourth-gen Spaceborne Computer to the Moon aboard Astrolab’s Flex Lunar Innovation Platform (FLIP) lunar rover. Part of NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) program, the rover is set to be deployed near the Moon’s south pole by the Voyager Technologies Griffin-1 lander later this year. Assuming a safe landing on the surface, FLIP will serve as a test bed for a range of emerging technologies including HPE’s latest space-faring compute platform. Specifically, Spaceborne Computer 4, which for the sake of brevity we’ll just call SBC4, will carry out a number of AI and HPC-centric experiments during the rover’s year long mission on the lunar pole. What we know about SBC4 so far The actual silicon powering SBC4 is still a bit of a mystery. We’re told the reason for the secrecy largely comes down to the high-risk nature of the mission. If the hardware fails, HPE’s compute partner doesn’t want their name tied to it. No guts but for the glory, we suppose, though Kioxia doesn't seem too worried. What we do know is that it is equipped with a low-power central processing unit, a graphics processor, and will be equipped with a pair of mirrored Kioxia SSDs totaling 1 TB of capacity. That said, while it'll be among the most powerful computers on the Moon, it's still a pretty small system. The FLIP rover doesn't have an unlimited power or thermal budget. The rover's radiators can only dissipate so much heat. item.content:encoded: Forget space datacenters. Before the end of the year, HPE will have AI running on the Moon. This isn’t some exec’s loony fantasy either. HPE has been building orbital compute platforms for the International Space Station (ISS) for years. Now, it’s sending its fourth-gen Spaceborne Computer to the Moon aboard Astrolab’s Flex Lunar Innovation Platform (FLIP) lunar rover. Part of NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) program, the rover is set to be deployed near the Moon’s south pole by the Voyager Technologies Griffin-1 lander later this year. Assuming a safe landing on the surface, FLIP will serve as a test bed for a range of emerging technologies including HPE’s latest space-faring compute platform. Specifically, Spaceborne Computer 4, which for the sake of brevity we’ll just call SBC4, will carry out a number of AI and HPC-centric experiments during the rover’s year long mission on the lunar pole. What we know about SBC4 so far The actual silicon powering SBC4 is still a bit of a mystery. We’re told the reason for the secrecy largely comes down to the high-risk nature of the mission. If the hardware fails, HPE’s compute partner doesn’t want their name tied to it. No guts but for the glory, we suppose, though Kioxia doesn't seem too worried. What we do know is that it is equipped with a low-power central processing unit, a graphics processor, and will be equipped with a pair of mirrored Kioxia SSDs totaling 1 TB of capacity. That said, while it'll be among the most powerful computers on the Moon, it's still a pretty small system. The FLIP rover doesn't have an unlimited power or thermal budget. The rover's radiators can only dissipate so much heat. Measuring in at around 5x10 inches and about an inch thick, while not a particularly big system, it's still large enough to house any number of existing compute platforms. For all we know, it could be powered by Nvidia’s GB10, AMD’s Xilinx Versal AI, or the guts of an old smartphone. We won't know until the thing powers up. Less of a mystery is what SBC4 will be running and where. NASA plans to run a series of tuned LLM tests on the system, including a retrieval augmented generation (RAG) system to assist with searching and interpreting onboard documents. Additionally, the system will be tasked with running machine learning algorithms against camera and LiDAR data. However, without knowing how large these LLMs are, it’s hard to infer the nature of the underlying hardware. We’re told to expect more details about the chips powering SBC4 once it’s up and running. Alongside AI, SBC4 will also run several high performance computing (HPC) benchmarks designed to push the system to its limits. These benchmarks include high performance Linpack (HPL) and high performance conjugate gradient (HPCG), which means HPE and Astrolab will soon hold the distinction of the first Top500 submission made from a celestial body. Not only do HPE’s systems power some of the fastest supercomputers on Earth, but they could soon hold the number one spot on the Moon — not that that’s a particularly high bar. Beyond bragging rights, a workload like HPL could have other benefits like helping to keep the rover from icing over during the roughly 14-day-long night cycles the rover will repeatedly endure over the course of its mission. Hardening SBC4 for the Moon The Rover and by extension SBC4 will have to contend with extreme vibration stresses during launch and landing, wild temperature swings, not to mention cosmic rays and solar radiation since the Moon lacks the thick atmosphere and magnetic field that shields terrestrial compute. But, as it turns out, radiation might not be as big a problem as you’d think. According to Fernandez, SBC4 is largely assembled from off-the-shelf components, including the solid state drives. The compute platform is using standard Kioxia BG6 M.2 drives with the main line of protection being a software RAID 1. “It’s a silent mirror. The boot order is to try this and if something has happened to it, go here,” Mark Fernandez, HPE’s chief scientist of space tech and solutions, explained. “With our nine years' experience in the Space Station using drives, we’ve even convinced them we don’t need to do anything special for space.” However, this wasn’t always the thinking. As we reported at the time, early Spaceborne Computers suffered from high SSD failure rates. But as it turned out, so did the same drives deployed terrestrially. The cause of the failures wasn’t cosmic rays or energetic particles from the Sun, but rather bad capacitors, he explained. “I’ve had zero SSD failure since 2019.” While off-the-shelf electronics are surprisingly radiation resistant — at least within FLIP’s mission parameters — HPE has invested heavily in software based redundancy and recovery. Fernandez calls this “hardware hardening in software.” The idea being that the spare CPU cycles are used to continuously monitor and compare hardware metrics against a state table. If a parameter exceeds the specified threshold, SBC4 will take action to protect itself. “At a high level, I say, I like to be running at full speed. I can't do that. I'll run at a slower speed. If I can't do that, I'd like to be booted, but not running anything, and then maybe the server will recover. And worst case, I'd like to be powered down rather than get destroyed,” he explained. At the edge of the edge FLIP is primarily intended as a proof of concept vehicle, which is to say it’s a test bed for technologies that may eventually find their way to the Moon on other missions. The inclusion of SBC4 reflects the realities of operating at the far edge of Earth’s orbit. The latency between Earth and the Moon is nowhere near as bad as Mars's up to 44 minute round-trip communication time, but even 2.5 seconds makes real-time control from Houston, or in this case Astrolab’s mission control, which by the way is also powered by HPE's Greenlake Private Cloud stack, in Hawthorne, California a bit unwieldy. Further complicating matters is the bandwidth afforded the rover. When Artemis 2 traveled around the Moon earlier this year, astronauts weren’t able to send back high-res photographs in real time due to the lack of bandwidth. It was only after the mission was on its way back to Earth that they were able to establish a big enough pipe to transmit the full-res images. For this reason, SBC4 is designed to operate “at the edge of the edge,” Fernandez said. Given the bandwidth constraints, it’s far easier to process as much of the data and telemetry gathered by the rover’s array of cameras, lidars, and environmental sensors locally. “It’s important to ship back insight to Earth rather than all the raw data whenever possible. So having the edge compute capability to process the raw data locally, save on bandwidth back to Earth,” Astrolab CEO Jaret Matthews said. Matthews isn’t the only one to share this perspective. Earlier this year, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang described the challenges and opportunities of space-based computing with analysts during the company’s Q1 earnings call. "There are many different computing problems that really want to be done in space," he said at the time. "One of the best use cases of GPUs in space is imaging. To be able to do imaging at very large, very high resolutions, extremely large scales and very, very fast, it's hard to do that by sending petabytes and petabytes of imaging data back here on Earth and doing that work, it's easier just to do it out in space." Though others' ambitions are far greater. Google, Amazon, and SpaceX are all touting orbital datacenters powered by the Sun as the answer to terrestrial power constraints — Elon Musk wants you to believe he'll eventually be manufacturing deep-space datacenters on the Moon and lobbing them into the far reaches of the solar system using mass drivers — the economics of getting those bit barns into low Earth orbit remain unproven and so far unviable. item.title: We Explored Uganda With ADCCE 2026, From Lake Victoria to Murchison Falls | See Photos
item.description: One minute, you’re dressed up for a beautiful dinner overlooking Lake Victoria. A few days later, you’re on a safari, watching wildlife in its natural habitat, cruising along the River Nile and getting an up-close view of one of Uganda’s most famous waterfalls. That’s how our trip to Uganda went, and we have so much to tell you. We travelled to Uganda, popularly known as the Pearl of Africa, for the inaugural Africa Destination Celebrations Conference & Expo (ADCCE) 2026, held from 12 to 13 October at the Speke Resort Munyonyo Convention Centre in Kampala, with familiarisation trips following the conference. The theme, Africa Unveils Events in the Wild, was an invitation to explore Africa’s potential as a destination for weddings, celebrations, luxury travel and unforgettable experiences. And after spending five days between Kampala and Murchison Falls National Park, we got to experience some of that potential ourselves. Our BellaNaija crew consisted of Oluwadunsin Sanya , our Head of Editorial and Innovation, who also serves on ADCCE’s Board of Directors; Dorcas Anya , our Senior HR and Operations Associate; and me, Funmilola Sanya , Senior Content Associate. First Stop: Lake Victoria, New Connections and a Dinner to Remember Our ADCCE experience began right at the airport, where the team welcomed us warmly to Uganda. It was a lovely introduction to the trip, and we were ready to see what the days ahead had in store. We settled into Speke Resort Munyonyo, the conference venue, where event planners, wedding professionals, hospitality experts, tourism operators and creatives from different parts of Africa and beyond had gathered to connect and share ideas. Day one was all about business-to-business meetings, meeting industry professionals and exploring what the exhibitors had to offer. It was a great opportunity to make new connections and discover more about the possibilities for destination celebrations across Africa. Then came lunch at Sunset Restaurant, overlooking Lake Victoria. I had a whole tilapia fish with sides, while some of my fellow delegates opted for chicken. With delicious food and that beautiful lake view, lunch was certainly a lovely way to spend the afternoon. Later that evening, we gathered for the Sound of Africa Dinner. Dressed in smart-casual white, delegates had another opportunity to mingle, enjoy the music and dance. item.content:encoded: One minute, you’re dressed up for a beautiful dinner overlooking Lake Victoria. A few days later, you’re on a safari, watching wildlife in its natural habitat, cruising along the River Nile and getting an up-close view of one of Uganda’s most famous waterfalls. That’s how our trip to Uganda went, and we have so much to tell you. We travelled to Uganda, popularly known as the Pearl of Africa, for the inaugural Africa Destination Celebrations Conference & Expo (ADCCE) 2026, held from 12 to 13 October at the Speke Resort Munyonyo Convention Centre in Kampala, with familiarisation trips following the conference. The theme, Africa Unveils Events in the Wild, was an invitation to explore Africa’s potential as a destination for weddings, celebrations, luxury travel and unforgettable experiences. And after spending five days between Kampala and Murchison Falls National Park, we got to experience some of that potential ourselves. Our BellaNaija crew consisted of Oluwadunsin Sanya , our Head of Editorial and Innovation, who also serves on ADCCE’s Board of Directors; Dorcas Anya , our Senior HR and Operations Associate; and me, Funmilola Sanya , Senior Content Associate. First Stop: Lake Victoria, New Connections and a Dinner to Remember Our ADCCE experience began right at the airport, where the team welcomed us warmly to Uganda. It was a lovely introduction to the trip, and we were ready to see what the days ahead had in store. We settled into Speke Resort Munyonyo, the conference venue, where event planners, wedding professionals, hospitality experts, tourism operators and creatives from different parts of Africa and beyond had gathered to connect and share ideas. Day one was all about business-to-business meetings, meeting industry professionals and exploring what the exhibitors had to offer. It was a great opportunity to make new connections and discover more about the possibilities for destination celebrations across Africa. Then came lunch at Sunset Restaurant, overlooking Lake Victoria. I had a whole tilapia fish with sides, while some of my fellow delegates opted for chicken. With delicious food and that beautiful lake view, lunch was certainly a lovely way to spend the afternoon. Later that evening, we gathered for the Sound of Africa Dinner. Dressed in smart-casual white, delegates had another opportunity to mingle, enjoy the music and dance. You know we weren’t going to travel all the way to Uganda and spend every evening sitting quietly. Between the conversations, music and laughter, it was a lovely start to our ADCCE adventure. Day Two: Big Conversations About Africa’s Celebration Industry The second day brought us back to the conference venue for conversations about positioning Africa as a global destination for celebrations. ADCCE founder Jackline Nanteza shared how attending a similar event had inspired her to believe that African event planners could one day come together to showcase the continent to the world. The first panel explored selling Destination Africa to the global market and the challenges of attracting international events. Oruonye Kingsley Chimezie championed Africa as a destination for celebrations, while Farah Lodhi reminded attendees, “What I believe is that in events, nothing is impossible as long as you don’t give up.” Rahul Soman highlighted how photography and social media can bring Africa’s destinations closer to couples worldwide, while Carol Matibiri reflected on the influence of international destination marketing. The second panel, “Uganda’s Event-Ready Hospitality Ecosystem,” moderated by Kemi Omeke , brought together representatives from NIRA, Uganda Tourism Board, Entikko Safari Lodge and UACII, alongside Frank Murangwa and Amos Wekesa , to discuss the partnerships needed to support events in Uganda. By evening, it was time for the black-tie VIP Networking Dinner, rounding off the conference with more opportunities to connect before our adventure continued into the wild. Next Stop: Murchison Falls National Park After the conference, we joined the familiarisation trip to Murchison Falls National Park. Getting there meant a long road trip from Kampala, filled with conversations, music courtesy of our DJ, Dorcas, laughter and Uganda’s changing scenery. We stayed at Entikko Safari Lodge, a beautiful retreat surrounded by nature. The food was another highlight, with so much to eat between our outings. Then came the safari the next morning. We spotted lions, giraffes, elephants, buffaloes and antelopes roaming the park. On our boat ride along the River Nile, we saw hippos and crocodiles in the water, offering us an even closer look at Uganda’s wildlife. Of course, we also visited Murchison Falls, often described as the world’s most powerful waterfall. Here, the River Nile squeezes through a gorge roughly seven metres wide before plunging about 43 metres. Seeing the rushing water and hearing its thunderous sound in person was an unforgettable experience. Between the wildlife, the breathtaking scenery and the delicious meals at Entikko, our Uganda adventure gave us plenty of memories to take home. One of my favourite parts of this trip was getting to experience Uganda with Oluwadunsin and Dorcas. Of course, we travelled for work, and ADCCE gave us the opportunity to meet professionals, learn about the destination celebrations industry and discover what different African businesses are creating. But there was also room to have fun together. We danced, laughed, explored new places, enjoyed the scenery and shared experiences that we’ll probably still be talking about long after returning home. And that’s one thing I appreciated about the structure of ADCCE 2026. The conference introduced us to the possibilities within Africa’s celebration and hospitality industries, while the familiarisation trip allowed us to see a destination beyond its meeting rooms and event venues. Uganda showed us its lakeside hospitality, its natural landscapes, its wildlife and some of the experiences that could make it an exciting choice for travellers and event organisers looking for something different. Until Next Time, Uganda! ADCCE 2026 brought together professionals with a shared interest in how Africa can welcome the world for celebrations, weddings, conferences and travel experiences. From the business conversations at Speke Resort Munyonyo to the adventures at Murchison Falls, the five-day experience gave us a lot to think about and even more to remember. We arrived in Uganda for a conference and left with new connections, fresh ideas, plenty of photographs and some wonderful travel memories. And if there’s one thing this trip has done, it’s given us even more reasons to explore Africa. item.title: 'Password1' and a forgotten test account land Welsh outfits in hot water
item.description: A test account protected by "Password1" helped an intruder steal personal data relating to 3,300 people, mostly children, in a ransomware attack that has drawn regulatory rebukes for two Welsh organizations. The Information Commission's Office (ICO) issued reprimands rather than fines to Ogi Networks Limited (ONL) and the Local Government Data Unit – Wales, also known as Data Cymru. According to the ICO, altnet ONL provided server and connectivity infrastructure, licensing, and support to Data Cymru, which helps public bodies across Wales make effective use of data. On November 1, 2024, Data Cymru suffered a ransomware attack after a miscreant exploited a test account called Test2 to infiltrate its network and encrypt 182.7 GB of data housed in a file server and an internal database server. "Before deploying the ransomware, the threat actor exfiltrated 42 GB of data from a primary domain controller, a file server and an SQL server," the ICO said on Tuesday in its reprimand of ONL [PDF]. ONL told the ICO it created the test account on January 13, 2012, during its initial project for Data Cymru. "ONL confirmed that the creation of the 'Test2' account was likely intended to test user account access before migrating 'real' users to its services," the ICO said. "When it was created, the 'Test2' account was given the password of 'Password1'." The ICO cited Bitwarden's password strength tool, which rated "Password1" as "very weak" and estimated a cracking time of less than a second. "The local administrator accounts on the three impacted systems all had the same password. This meant that once one system had been breached, the local account hashes could be collected and used by the threat actor to authenticate access to other systems on the Data Cymru network," the regulator added. "ONL confirmed that it did not carry out any reviews of local administrator accounts following their initial deployment. This meant these accounts remained active, regardless of whether they were used, and continued to use the same default passwords set at the time of their creation in January 2012, as part of ONL's initial project with Data Cymru, for more than 12.5 years." The data watchdog reprimanded ONL under Article 32 of the UK GDPR because it failed to put in place "appropriate technical and organisational measures" to ensure processing systems and services were safe, and it didn't regularly assess or evaluate those measures. It found ONL had no auditing procedures to review user accounts within Data Cymru's Active Directory. The ICO's separate reprimand of Data Cymru [PDF] also detailed failures in its security arrangements. "Password1 is not an appropriate password, it is a wide-open door to nefarious actors," said ICO head of investigations David Doodson. "This incident shows how a single weak password, attached to an account that was no longer needed, can leave the door open to a serious cyber-attack that can affect thousands. item.title: Beyond the Summit: How Glo Is Building Culture of Support, Growth for Women
item.description: For many women, professional growth is shaped not only by the opportunities available to them but also by the communities that encourage them to pursue those opportunities, recognise their achievements and support them through different stages of their journeys. At Globacom , this understanding continues to shape SheGlows , an internal women’s community designed to foster meaningful connections, shared learning and personal and professional development. The community’s commitment to these values took centre stage at the third edition of the SheGlows Summit, held on October 17, 2026, at the Mike Adenuga Centre, Ikoyi, Lagos. With the theme Lead. Thrive. Grow. , the summit brought together women from across the organisation to exchange experiences, gain fresh perspectives and explore how they can continue to grow as individuals, professionals and members of a supportive community. While the annual summit provides an opportunity for reflection and connection, the broader significance of SheGlows lies in its continued efforts to create opportunities for women beyond a single event. Since its introduction in 2025, the SheGlows Scholarship Fund has supported four women, with two beneficiaries each year. The community’s mentorship programme, now in its second cohort, also provides a platform for women to share knowledge, learn from experience and strengthen their professional capabilities. Together, these initiatives reflect Globacom’s approach to women’s development, combining opportunities for learning with the relationships and support systems that encourage sustained growth. The community benefits from the support of Globacom’s leadership, including Chairman Dr Mike Adenuga Jr ., whose commitment to employee development has helped create an enabling environment for initiatives focused on building the capabilities of the company’s people. In a goodwill message presented at the summit by Esther John , Head of Strategy, Office of the Executive Vice Chairman, Globacom’s Executive Vice Chairman, Bella Disu , encouraged women to recognise their potential, embrace opportunities for continuous development and strengthen the relationships that help communities thrive. She emphasized that leadership was not limited to formal positions but could be demonstrated through the difference individuals make wherever they find themselves. This message was echoed in remarks by Jumobi Mofe-Damijo , Chair of the SheGlows community, who drew attention to the importance of recognising and celebrating the women who actively contribute to its growth. She observed that establishing a community was only the beginning, noting that its strength depended on the willingness of members to participate, support one another and celebrate collective achievements. Her remarks reinforced one of the central ideas behind SheGlows: that a thriving community is built not simply through programmes and activities but through the relationships, contributions and shared experiences of its member

item.content:encoded: For many women, professional growth is shaped not only by the opportunities available to them but also by the communities that encourage them to pursue those opportunities, recognise their achievements and support them through different stages of their journeys. At Globacom , this understanding continues to shape SheGlows , an internal women’s community designed to foster meaningful connections, shared learning and personal and professional development. The community’s commitment to these values took centre stage at the third edition of the SheGlows Summit, held on October 17, 2026, at the Mike Adenuga Centre, Ikoyi, Lagos. With the theme Lead. Thrive. Grow. , the summit brought together women from across the organisation to exchange experiences, gain fresh perspectives and explore how they can continue to grow as individuals, professionals and members of a supportive community. While the annual summit provides an opportunity for reflection and connection, the broader significance of SheGlows lies in its continued efforts to create opportunities for women beyond a single event. Since its introduction in 2025, the SheGlows Scholarship Fund has supported four women, with two beneficiaries each year. The community’s mentorship programme, now in its second cohort, also provides a platform for women to share knowledge, learn from experience and strengthen their professional capabilities. Together, these initiatives reflect Globacom’s approach to women’s development, combining opportunities for learning with the relationships and support systems that encourage sustained growth. The community benefits from the support of Globacom’s leadership, including Chairman Dr Mike Adenuga Jr ., whose commitment to employee development has helped create an enabling environment for initiatives focused on building the capabilities of the company’s people. In a goodwill message presented at the summit by Esther John , Head of Strategy, Office of the Executive Vice Chairman, Globacom’s Executive Vice Chairman, Bella Disu , encouraged women to recognise their potential, embrace opportunities for continuous development and strengthen the relationships that help communities thrive. She emphasized that leadership was not limited to formal positions but could be demonstrated through the difference individuals make wherever they find themselves. This message was echoed in remarks by Jumobi Mofe-Damijo , Chair of the SheGlows community, who drew attention to the importance of recognising and celebrating the women who actively contribute to its growth. She observed that establishing a community was only the beginning, noting that its strength depended on the willingness of members to participate, support one another and celebrate collective achievements. Her remarks reinforced one of the central ideas behind SheGlows: that a thriving community is built not simply through programmes and activities but through the relationships, contributions and shared experiences of its members. The summit’s three guest speakers brought this philosophy to life through conversations on leadership, professional presence and personal aspirations. Dr Kehinde Nwani , Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Meadow Hall Group, encouraged participants to recognise that leadership begins with personal responsibility and the willingness to make a difference, regardless of one’s position. Nneka Jethro-Iruobe , a human resources and rewards expert and former Director of People & Change at KPMG, explored how initiative, accountability and professional presence can shape individual effectiveness and career development. Grace Ofure Ibhakhomu , Chief Executive Officer of Lifecard Investment Company Nigeria and Lifecard Dubai, challenged participants to look beyond their present circumstances and approach their aspirations with vision, resilience and long-term thinking. Together, the conversations reflected the summit’s theme, encouraging participants to see leadership, fulfilment and growth as interconnected aspects of their personal and professional journeys. The programme also featured an interactive panel discussion moderated by lawyer and media personality Olive Emodi , providing participants with an opportunity to engage the speakers and share perspectives on the challenges and opportunities women encounter. In her closing remarks, Kemi Fadipe encouraged participants to sustain the connections and lessons from the summit, reinforcing the importance of continued learning and mutual support. For Globacom, the significance of SheGlows extends beyond the success of its annual gathering. Guided by the principles of Support. Build. Mentor. , the community reflects an ongoing commitment to creating an environment where women can learn from one another, develop their capabilities and feel recognised for their contributions. As SheGlows continues to evolve, its combination of mentorship, educational support and community engagement offers an example of how organisations can foster a workplace culture in which women’s development is encouraged not only through formal opportunities but also through connection, recognition and collective progress. item.title: See The Nominees for the 2026 Future Awards Africa!
item.description: Credit: The Future Awards Africa As always, the Future Awards Africa continues to celebrate young Africans who are making a difference across industries, from entertainment and media to technology, business, advocacy, content creation, performing arts and more. Over the years, the awards have become an important platform for recognising the ideas, talent and achievements of young people contributing the continent’s present and future. item.title: Google Cloud says a 'power event' caused today's outage
item.description: UPDATED Google Cloud has blamed a “power event” for taking down multiple online products for customers in Western Europe, and is pledging to restore normal service within the hour. The unplanned downtime for customers began at 0608 UTC when europe-west-2-b, one of three local availability zones in the London region, started playing up. According to an update on its status page , Google Cloud said at 1158 UTC that full recovery workloads should be “completed, tentatively” by 1300 UTC. Customers can expect another update at that point, with Google either giving the thumbs up, thumbs sideways or having to admit engineers are still working on a fix. Services that went AWOL included BigQuery Data TransferService, Cloud Filestore, Cloud Run, Google App Engine, Google Cloud NetApp Volumes, Google Kubernetes Engine, and Managed Service for Apache Kafka. So what caused online services to melt at customers including Lloyds Bank, HSBC, Royal Mail, Rightmove, DPD, BT, Screwfix and Revolut? Power. "A power event caused an outage within europe-west2-b zone. The power event is mitigated. We are seeing the recovery of services and are prioritizing the recovery of existing workloads.Customers may not be able to yet create new workloads." The Register has asked Google for further elucidation but it said the only information is available on the status page. The "fragility" of the cloud model is again on display, Dr Amro Al-Said Ahmad , a lecturer in computer science at Keele University told The Register . He estimates that a total of 38 services were down and out for the count. "The incident highlights the dependency effect of modern cloud ecosystems. When a core cloud region experiences failures, the impact extends far beyond the directly affected services. Applications, APIs, databases, authentication systems, payment platforms, analytics pipelines, and third-party SaaS products that depend on those services can all experience cascading failures." "A problem in a single cloud region can therefore propagate through an entire digital supply chain, affecting organisations that are several layers removed from the original outage. While this is a regional outage centered on europe-west2, the breadth of affected services highlights a key cloud engineering lesson: resilience is not achieved by simply moving to the cloud. True resilience requires designing for regional failures through multi-region deployments, workload portability, and tested disaster recovery procedures." Updated at 17.37 UTC on October 20, 2026, to add: Google's status page says it mostly ironed out the wrinkles at 14.03 UTC and normal service resumed for the majority of customers. "The issue with impacted GCP products has been mitigated for most of the customers and it is believed to be affecting currently a very small number of customers and our Engineering Team is working on it." item.title: I’m a CTO. AI still needs your human expertise | Madhu Shashanka
item.description: AI is increasingly getting good at doing some tasks, but it can never replace human workers’ judgment Autonomous cars, which may be the safest we have built, keep getting easily avoidable parking tickets. While Waymos crash far less often than human drivers over tens of millions of miles, they’re still terrible at performing basic tasks – keeping out of disabled parking spots and tow-away zones, or steering clear of a church garage during Sunday service, according to the Wall Street Journal . That is the state of AI today: impressively capable at something complex, yet embarrassingly clumsy at something easy. And it has implications for what work will remain human and what will be automated by AI. Madhu Shashanka is co-founder, chief scientist and chief technology officer at Concentric AI, a data security software company Continue reading...

item.title: How Brazil’s election result could shape women’s football in the country
item.description: Female players including Carlinha and Tayla Carolina have spoken out against the far right, who they fear will harm the women’s game as well as wider society The day before the first round of Brazilian elections, the Estádio do Morumbi hosted the second leg of the Brazilian Women’s Championship final, in which São Paulo drew 1-1 with Corinthians to win 3-2 on aggregate and secure the Brasileirão Women’s title. It had been an incredible final but after the game the goalkeeper Carlinha used an interview to appeal to her fans: “Never again Bolsonaro in power,” she shouted to a record-breaking TV audience of 23 million people. Continue reading...

item.title: Bullhorn sees red after cyberattack knocks recruitment platform offline
item.description: Bullhorn is the latest tech giant finding itself on the wrong end of a cyberattack, forcing the recruitment software provider to shut down its platform while it investigates. The US-based company, which serves more than 10,000 customers worldwide, says its systems are now back online in the UK, US, and Australia. Unfortunately for customers hoping to get back to work, online doesn't necessarily mean working. In its latest status update, published on Tuesday , Bullhorn confirmed that some users were still struggling with single sign-on (SSO), password resets, and customizations, while several products continued to report degraded performance. Things started going sideways on Friday, October 16, when Bullhorn flagged problems getting job postings onto Indeed. By the following morning, the platform was suffering a full-blown outage, and Bullhorn confirmed later that day that it was dealing with something rather more serious than a technical hiccup. "We have detected a cyber incident on the Bullhorn Platform. We have temporarily disabled access to our systems in order to contain the activity while we investigate further," the company said, noting that it had roped in cybersecurity specialists from CrowdStrike to help investigate the attack and restore its services. For recruitment agencies using Bullhorn, the outage meant losing access to candidate records, job applications, placements and, in some cases, the systems used to get people paid. Services began returning on Monday, but recovery has been anything but seamless. As of Tuesday morning, Bullhorn's status page still listed degraded performance across several products, including its automation tools, Talent Platform, Onboarding365 and Time & Expense. While Bullhorn is making progress getting customers back into their accounts, it has yet to answer arguably the bigger question: whether the attackers stole anything. In its customer FAQ , it said a forensic investigation is ongoing, and has not yet determined whether attackers exfiltrated customer data. Bullhorn says it will contact affected customers if the investigation finds their information was compromised, and it also warned people to watch out for opportunistic crooks looking to exploit the chaos. "Threat actors may pose as Bullhorn personnel via email, text, or phone calls, using the incident as a pretext to request credentials or sensitive information," it warned on Tuesday, stressing that its employees would never ask customers to disclose passwords, multi-factor authentication codes, or verification tokens. The company has also required password resets for users who don’t log in through SSO, while customers using API integrations have been instructed to rotate their credentials. The cause of the intrusion remains unknown, and Bullhorn has not publicly identified the attackers or confirmed whether ransomware was involved. item.title: Could a $200K bond for satellites paid before launch prevent a space junk disaster in orbit? Here's why some scientists think so
item.description:
Tereza is a London-based science and technology journalist, aspiring fiction writer and amateur gymnast. Originally from Prague, the Czech Republic, she spent the first seven years of her career working as a reporter, script-writer and presenter for various TV programmes of the Czech Public Service Television. She later took a career break to pursue further education and added a Master's in Science from the International Space University, France, to her Bachelor's in Journalism and Master's in Cultural Anthropology from Prague's Charles University. She worked as a reporter at the Engineering and Technology magazine, freelanced for a range of publications including Live Science, Space.com, Professional Engineering, Via Satellite and Space News and served as a maternity cover science editor at the European Space Agency.

The space around Earth is turning into a junkyard. Researchers think a refundable deposit scheme could force satellite operators to clean up their act before a tipping point is reached. For years, space sustainability experts have warned that the growing number of satellites in orbit and the quantity of dead metal left behind threatens to trigger a dangerous cascade of collisions known as the Kessler Syndrome . Predicted in the 1970s by NASA physicist Donald Kessler, this chain of orbital smashups could make the space around Earth unusable and unsafe. The dangerous tipping might be nearer than some think. Humankind's utilization of space is at an inflection point, as companies such as SpaceX , Blue Origin and Amazon plan to launch constellations of hundreds of thousands of telecommunication satellites and orbiting data centers in the coming years. " Low Earth orbit looks like lots of other resources that we have trashed as economic actors," Daniel Kaffine, a professor of environmental and resource economics at University of Colorado Boulder, told Space.com. "Waiting until it gets really, really bad to start implementing any of these types of policy interventions has historically been what we have done," Kaffine added. "But maybe we can think about things we can do right now." In a paper published last month in the journal Nature Communications, Kaffine and his collaborators propose a scheme that would require satellite operators to post a bond of $200,000 before launch, refundable with interest upon the completion of a successful deorbit. Companies that fail to remove their junk would lose the money, which could go toward a shared pool funding active debris-removal missions , the researchers said. "You could possibly raise billions of dollars by that," said Kaffine. "We think it's a very neat policy that doesn't require international coordination." International bodies, such as the Inter-Agency Space Debris Coordination Committee, ask satellite operators to remove their spacecraft from orbit within 25 years after the mission's end. item.content:encoded:
Tereza is a London-based science and technology journalist, aspiring fiction writer and amateur gymnast. Originally from Prague, the Czech Republic, she spent the first seven years of her career working as a reporter, script-writer and presenter for various TV programmes of the Czech Public Service Television. She later took a career break to pursue further education and added a Master's in Science from the International Space University, France, to her Bachelor's in Journalism and Master's in Cultural Anthropology from Prague's Charles University. She worked as a reporter at the Engineering and Technology magazine, freelanced for a range of publications including Live Science, Space.com, Professional Engineering, Via Satellite and Space News and served as a maternity cover science editor at the European Space Agency.

The space around Earth is turning into a junkyard. Researchers think a refundable deposit scheme could force satellite operators to clean up their act before a tipping point is reached. For years, space sustainability experts have warned that the growing number of satellites in orbit and the quantity of dead metal left behind threatens to trigger a dangerous cascade of collisions known as the Kessler Syndrome . Predicted in the 1970s by NASA physicist Donald Kessler, this chain of orbital smashups could make the space around Earth unusable and unsafe. The dangerous tipping might be nearer than some think. Humankind's utilization of space is at an inflection point, as companies such as SpaceX , Blue Origin and Amazon plan to launch constellations of hundreds of thousands of telecommunication satellites and orbiting data centers in the coming years. " Low Earth orbit looks like lots of other resources that we have trashed as economic actors," Daniel Kaffine, a professor of environmental and resource economics at University of Colorado Boulder, told Space.com. "Waiting until it gets really, really bad to start implementing any of these types of policy interventions has historically been what we have done," Kaffine added. "But maybe we can think about things we can do right now." In a paper published last month in the journal Nature Communications, Kaffine and his collaborators propose a scheme that would require satellite operators to post a bond of $200,000 before launch, refundable with interest upon the completion of a successful deorbit. Companies that fail to remove their junk would lose the money, which could go toward a shared pool funding active debris-removal missions , the researchers said. "You could possibly raise billions of dollars by that," said Kaffine. "We think it's a very neat policy that doesn't require international coordination." International bodies, such as the Inter-Agency Space Debris Coordination Committee, ask satellite operators to remove their spacecraft from orbit within 25 years after the mission's end. The American Federal Communications Commission (FCC) imposes an even stricter standard — a five-year requirement for satellites in low Earth orbit. Still, a staggering 60% of satellites remain in place when their propellant runs out, the researchers say, as no consequences ensue if they fail to deorbit. Solving the problem on the international level would be difficult, as international bodies have no powers to enforce compliance. Moreover, the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS), which sets down rules for the peaceful exploration of outer space, requires the unanimous support of every member state to pass new regulations, which is nearly impossible to achieve. "The policy we propose could be implemented on a national level, which is why we think it's interesting," Indigo Brownhall, a space sustainability researcher at University College London and the paper's lead author, told Space.com. "Any country in Europe can request satellites registered with them to follow this bond policy." To put it simply, no satellite registered in a given country gets to space before putting the money into the kitty. The researchers acknowledge that it might be hard to persuade major players historically averse to regulations, such as the U.S., to roll out such a scheme. But they say a more environmentally conscious block, like the European Union (EU), could enforce compliance by limiting market access to those who observe their rules. "The consumer market in Europe is massive, like 300 to 400 million people," Brownhall said. "And the EU can request anyone who wants to sell space data or any products in the EU to follow their rules. They did this with GDPR [General Data Protection Regulation]. And you can imagine that somebody like Starlink [SpaceX's satellite-internet subsidiary] surely wants to sell Starlink terminals to Europeans." The authors estimate that, even if the scheme only covered 20% of global satellite launches, it would reduce the number of derelict satellites careening around the planet by 18%. An old rocket body tumbles in space above Earth as seen from Japan's Astroscale ADRAS-J satellite. (Image credit: Astroscale) Currently, more than 57,000 pieces of space debris larger than 4 inches (10 centimeters) hurtle around Earth completely out of control, according to estimates by the European Space Agency. That's double the figure from less than 10 years ago. Most of these fragments were generated by explosions and orbital collisions that shattered satellites and used rocket stages into clouds of dangerous debris. "Leaving big satellites that no longer work up there is like a ticking time bomb," Brownhall said. "Active satellites can move out of the way, but when two derelict satellites are going to hit each other, there is nothing you can do but watch it." Kaffine said the policy could be modelled on U.S. oil operators' bond scheme, in place since the 1960s, which ensures that oil giants plug used oil wells after ceasing extraction. "If the oil operators clean up after completing the oil production job, they get the money back," said Kaffine. "If they don't, the money goes into a fund, which the government then uses to clean up orphan wells. It's quite an analogous situation to what we see in space." In the meantime, evidence of the worsening orbital situation is coming thick and fast. Space situational awareness companies such as U.S.-based LeoLabs , which use networks of ground-based radars and telescopes to monitor traffic in space, report increasing numbers of disintegration events — incidents involving either an explosion or a collision between old satellites, fragments and rocket bodies. In the past six months, LeoLabs has reported at least four fragmentation events in space, which together created hundreds of new pieces of space debris.

item.title: Microsoft admits that Always On VPN problems were not fixed in the October Security Update
item.description: Microsoft has been forced to admit that the Always On VPN glitch – which it said it had fixed in an update on October 13 – was not actually fixed after all. We've all been there. You fix that bug, or tweak the configuration setting, and you're pleased with yourself, but it turns out it didn't take, and you have to send the "er, about that fix" follow-up email of shame. The same has happened to Microsoft. After proudly declaring the problem resolved as part of its last security update , the company had to roll back its triumphant trumpeting to a sad little parp from a clown's horn in the message WI1482218: "This disclosure was mistakenly updated to Resolved status on October 13, 2026. We have returned its status to Mitigated. "We apologize for any inconvenience or confusion." The bug in question concerns the operating system's Always On VPN functionality, a useful bit of code that quietly opens a VPN connection in the background without tiresome prompts for authentication. It dates back to Windows 10, and Microsoft alerted administrators to problems after the September 2026 Windows security update inadvertently broke it. The issue affects Windows 11 versions from 24H2 through 26H2. The problem could occur when the VPN was set to try a different connection method if the initial connection failed (Microsoft gave the example of using automatic protocol selection with IKEv2 and SSTP). According to Microsoft: "Affected VPN connections might remain in a 'Connecting' state or repeatedly attempt to connect without succeeding. Subsequent connection attempts might also display the error: 'The specified port is already in use'." This is not ideal for administrators. The workaround Microsoft highlighted back on October 13 was to change from automatic protocol selection to a single protocol, which would at least get affected users up and running. The workaround remains the same. The bad news is that, because last week's fix did not work, affected administrators will need to apply the workaround for a bit longer. Microsoft claimed, "A resolution for this issue is planned to be included in an update to be released in the coming weeks." ®

item.title: SpaceX launches its 'Starfall' return capsule for 2nd time ever (video)
item.description: null SpaceX just launched its mysterious "Starfall" return capsule for the second time ever. Starfall was one of 32 payloads on the company's Bandwagon-5 rideshare mission, which launched atop a Falcon 9 rocket at 7:04 a.m. EDT (1104 GMT) today (Oct. 20) from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. SpaceX has been relatively quiet about Starfall, which debuted this past June on a Falcon 9 launch from the Cape. The payloads of SpaceX's Bandwagon-5 rideshare mission, seen in a prelaunch photo. The company's Starfall capsule sits at the very top of the stack. (Image credit: SpaceX) That June 23 flight was a dedicated demonstration mission for Starfall, designed to show that the capsule can fly in a controlled fashion and survive the harrowing downward trip through Earth's atmosphere . And those will be Starfall's main jobs. The vehicle "will enable affordable, routine access to the microgravity environment for scientific research and in-space manufacturing," SpaceX in a June 23 X post , one of the few public statements the company has made about Starfall. Indeed, most of the details that we have about the capsule come from an environmental assessment that was published by the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration in May. According to that document, the disk-shaped Starfall is roughly 2.5 feet (0.75 meters) tall and 10.2 feet (3.1 m) wide. It weighs about 4,600 pounds (2,100 kilograms) and can bring 2,200 pounds (1,000 kg) of payload back down to Earth. Artist's illustration of a SpaceX Starfall capsule reentering Earth's atmosphere. (Image credit: SpaceX) Starfall wasn't the only return capsule that went up on Bandwagon-5. Among the other 31 payloads on the flight was W-Series 7, the latest orbital "mini-factory" built and operated by the California company Varda Space Industries . The W-Series capsules are designed to both host the production of valuable goods such as pharmaceuticals and bring them safely down to Earth, Varda has said. The other payloads on Bandwagon-5 are a mix of " cubesats and microsats," according to SpaceX's mission description . Among the latter is Pelican-12 , a sharp-eyed Earth-observation satellite built by the San Francisco company Planet. Payload deployment sequence is complete October 20, 2026 The 32 payloads were deployed over a two-hour span beginning about 57 minutes after launch. Starfall will be the last to separate, releasing from the Falcon 9's upper stage two hours and 48 minutes post-liftoff. The Falcon 9's first stage, meanwhile, came back to Earth as planned on Bandwagon-5. It touched down about nine minutes after launch, coming down in the Atlantic Ocean atop the SpaceX drone ship "A Shortfall of Gravitas." It was the 19th mission for this particular booster, according to the company. (Image credit: SpaceX) Bandwagon is one of two SpaceX rideshare programs. The other, known as Transporter, has been busier, flying 18 missions to date . The first Transporter mission, which lifted off in January 2021, del

item.title: Whitehall shuts the front door on digital ID but leaves the back open
item.description: Britain's national digital ID scheme may be dead, but Whitehall appears to have forgotten to tell the infrastructure. Despite the government scrapping its controversial plans , officials told MPs on Monday that work continues on GOV.UK One Login, digital wallets, and a growing collection of digital credentials designed to help people prove who they are. The abandoned scheme was one of Keir Starmer's flagship policies, originally pitched as a compulsory digital ID card to crack down on illegal working. Privacy campaigners weren't impressed, warning of surveillance and government overreach, and ministers eventually made it voluntary before Andy Burnham, decided to bin the whole thing. But scrapping the scheme hasn't dented Whitehall's digital identity ambitions. Officials told MPs this week that more than 80 types of documents are earmarked for the government's digital wallet, including proof of benefits, driving test certificates, and Disclosure and Barring Service (DBS) certificates. That's quite a lot of paperwork for something that's supposedly dead. The revelations came during a Public Accounts Committee hearing on Monday, where MPs wanted to know what exactly had been scrapped. "But is it not the case, based on the answers you've given us this afternoon, that the infrastructure of digital ID in the public sector is still being pursued?" asked Sarah Green, Liberal Democrat MP for Chesham and Amersham. Susannah Storey, DCMS permanent secretary, was keen to draw a line between the national scheme ministers had scrapped and the digital identity projects Whitehall had no intention of abandoning. One Login already allows people to prove who they are online, she said, but "that is not the same as a national digital identity strategy." Rod Latham, DCMS director for cybersecurity and digital identity, had a convenient explanation for why so much of digital ID was still standing: the government had only scrapped plans for a new identity product. "We already had One Login and the Gov Wallet," he told MPs, adding that work on the digital identity trust framework was also underway before the national scheme was announced. Whitehall isn't wasting time putting that technology to use, with officials confirming that testing is already underway to enable digital credentials to work with private businesses. Natalie Jones, the senior responsible owner for GOV.UK One Login, revealed that the government had opened a testing environment for private sector providers to integrate with its digital wallet technology. This would let people use digital driving licenses to prove their age in pubs , collect parcels, or verify their identity online. "We've got a bit of a chicken and egg situation. A digital driving license is only useful if there are people ready and shops and businesses ready to receive it,” Jones said, noting that further testing is planned for December, with a national rollout of digital driving licenses targeted for 2027.
