Right between those two headline showers, the dependable Orionids take their turn, reaching peak activity around Oct. 21-22. So, when and where can you catch the show? When and where to watch Make sure you wrap up warm for a night of Orionid hunting. (Image credit: Created in Canva by Daisy Dobrijevic) The Orionids take their name from the spot where they seem to fan out: Orion's raised club, just above and to the left of the reddish star Betelgeuse. Orion is usually a winter favorite, so in early autumn the mighty hunter doesn't fully clear the eastern horizon until after 11 p.m. local daylight time. Don't rush outside just yet though. Wait until around 2 a.m., when Orion is well above the horizon. By about 5 a.m., just before dawn, Orion reaches its highest point in the southern sky — and the view should be at its best. Orionid meteors tend to be faint, so city lights can easily wash them out. If you can, head to a safe, dark rural spot. Get comfortable in a reclining lawn chair or sleeping bag, give your eyes time to adjust, and enjoy the view overhead and toward the southern sky. Why the moon won't spoil the show And what about the moon? A full moon arrives October 25-26, but there's still a welcome stretch of dark sky for several mornings before Wednesday. By Oct. 21-22, the waxing gibbous moon will be resting among the dim stars of Capricornus, reaching its highest point around 8:45 p.m. local daylight time. Here's the good news: it will set shortly after 2 a.m., leaving roughly 3½ hours of dark sky before dawn. In that window, one observer may spot as many as 15 to 20 Orionids per hour. Because those hours line up with the shower's peak, the moon shouldn't steal the show this year. Halley's Comet: the source of the Orionids So, where do the Orionids come from? Their story begins with Halley's Comet —the same famous visitor behind May's Eta Aquarids. Meteoroids are tiny leftovers from a comet's nucleus. As a comet nears the sun, frozen material on its surface turns directly into gas, a process known as sublimation. The comet becomes a kind of cosmic litterbug, sprinkling dust and debris along its orbit. Those pieces are tiny and brittle, with the consistency of cigar ash, and every swing past the sun leaves more behind. Comets are among the solar system's oldest and most fascinating objects. They formed alongside the sun and planets about 4.6 billion years ago, yet they have changed remarkably little. Think of them as time capsules from the solar system's childhood. Far beyond the outer planets, they spend most of their time in a deep freeze, where temperatures hover just above absolute zero , -459.67°F (-273.15°C). In that extreme cold, chemical reactions largely stop, helping comets preserve material from those earliest days. Over the past 100,000 years, Halley's Comet has probably circled the sun well over a thousand times, leaving a fresh trail of debris on every visit. Each October and May, Earth brushes close to Halley's orbit. Some of that dust meets our atmosphere at a breathtaking 41 miles (66 km) per second, lighting up as the streaks we call "shooting stars." The Orionids have another lovely feature: about half of these meteors leave glowing trails that linger longer than those of equally bright meteors. Halley's composition may be the reason. The particles begin burning up about 80 miles (130 km) above Earth, perhaps because they're made of lightweight material from the comet's diffuse surface rather than its core. Close-up view of Halley's Comet captured by the Giotto spacecraft in 1986. (Image credit: ESA. Courtesy of MPAe, Lindau) Looking backward . . . and forward Perhaps you remember seeing Halley's Comet when it last swept through the inner solar system in late winter and early spring of 1986. With an orbital period of 75.4 years, this celebrated visitor is due back in late July or early August 2061. For a little perspective, average life expectancy is 79.5 years in the United States, 82.2 years in the United Kingdom, and 83.4 years in Canada. So, if you were born after 1980, there's a fair chance you'll be here to welcome the "mother of all Orionids" home in 2061. As for me, I saw Halley in 1986 at the "advanced age" of 30. The odds of another reunion are pretty long — you can do the math. Until then, I'll be more than happy to step outside early on Wednesday morning and greet a few of "Halley's children." I hope you'll join me. Joe Rao serves as an instructor and guest lecturer at New York's Hayden Planetarium . He writes about astronomy for Natural History magazine , Sky and Telescope , The Old Farmer's Almanac and other publications.

item.title: Scientists find 'gemstones' in atmosphere of bizarre, scorching-hot 'marshmallow' exoplanet
item.description: null Using data from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), astronomers have unraveled some of the atmospheric secrets of a bizarre, blisteringly hot world that has the consistency of marshmallow. The extrasolar planet, or exoplanet , under the watchful infrared eye of the JWST , is WASP-17b, located around 1,300 light-years away. The exoplanet has a mass around 0.8 times that of Jupiter, but it is around twice as wide as the solar system's largest planet, giving it a "super-puff" consistency comparable to the Earth-based treat. WASP-17 b is so close to its parent star that it completes an orbit in under four Earth days, with this proximity also making the temperature of this " hot Jupiter " skyrocket. Given the extreme conditions of this exoplanet, it is little wonder that its atmosphere is pretty unusual too. Using a new technique called transmission strings, a team of scientists mapped the contours of the atmosphere of WASP-17b. They found that the atmosphere is shaped like a ring with prominent "gems" rising from it. "Planets are temperamental, their atmospheres complex and chaotic," team member Hannah Wakeford of the University of Bristol said in a statement. "The fact that all of these numbers came together and showed us this very structured, dynamical picture of this giant world over 1,000 light-years away was just really exciting." Astronomers like WASP-17b so much they put a ring on it WASP-17b is so close to its parent star that it is tidally locked, meaning one side permanently faces the star; its dayside is constantly bombarded with stellar radiation. In contrast, the planet also has a cooler nightside, which faces out into space in perpetuity. By creating incredibly comprehensive 3D views of this exoplanet's atmosphere, researchers found that WASP-17b's atmosphere has a chemical composition and temperature that shift between dayside and nightside according to theory and modelling. This was possible because the transmission strings technique tracked WASP-17b as it crossed or transited in front of its star, capturing the composition of light around the edge of the planet's atmosphere, or limb, from different angles. This method trumps standard approaches because traditional modelling only maps light as an average across the entire limb. "Rather than assuming your atmosphere is a circle with the same radius all the way around, our technique allows you to pull out different distances from the center to the edge of the planet," Lili Alderson, of Cornell University, said. "We're able to go around the edge. "So, we've gone from a ring to understanding where on the ring the gemstones are, so to speak." The modelling showed just such a "gem," that occurs where hot winds from the planet reach the equator and the nightside of WASP-17b, the atmosphere of the cooler side inflates. In contrast, the planet also has a cooler nightside, which faces out into space in perpetuity. This method trumps standard approaches because traditional modelling only maps light as an average across the entire limb. "Rather than assuming your atmosphere is a circle with the same radius all the way around, our technique allows you to pull out different distances from the center to the edge of the planet," Lili Alderson, of Cornell University, said. "We're able to go around the edge. "So, we've gone from a ring to understanding where on the ring the gemstones are, so to speak." The modelling showed just such a "gem," that occurs where hot winds from the planet reach the equator and the nightside of WASP-17b, the atmosphere of the cooler side inflates. An illustration of the atmosphere of WASP-17b with "gems" rising from it. (Image credit: Robert Lea) "Theory predicts that the morning and the evening sides should have a strong temperature difference, and WASP-17b fits really nicely in that trend – pretty much bang-on what we thought it would be," Alderson said. The successful application of the transmission strings method is an exciting step forward in the modelling of the atmospheres of the over 6,000 worlds in NASA's exoplanet catalog . "This is proof of concept that planets are, in fact, 3D objects, and that, consistently, as they go around their star, what we predict should be happening is happening," Alderson concluded. "To move beyond computational exercises and see it for real is a different matter." The team's research was published on Wednesday (Oct.14) in the journal Nature Astronomy.

item.title: The Real Flex Is Healthy Skin: Inside the Vaseline and Dove Experience at BITML 2026
item.description: From personalised skin consultations and hands-on product trials to picture-perfect Glow Cam portraits, Vaseline and Dove delivered a memorable experience at Beauty in the Motherland (BITML) 2026 . As sponsors, both brands made healthy skin the focus of the experience, inviting visitors to understand that “ The Real Flex Is Healthy Skin .” Held from 5–7 October at the Eko Convention Centre in Lagos, the event brought together Africa’s beauty professionals, brands, manufacturers, retailers, distributors, creators and consumers. Exhibitions and panel discussions explored everything from local manufacturing to skincare, haircare and the future of the continent’s beauty industry. Within that wider conversation, Vaseline and Dove encouraged beauty enthusiasts to move beyond simply following the latest skincare trend and spend time understanding their own skin. Their booth became a destination for visitors to get better acquainted with products they knew and discover others they could add to their routines. Vaseline’s and Dove’s pop-up booths stood out across the exhibition floor, drawing guests into an experience that encouraged them to ask, explore and try for themselves. At the Vaseline Skin Proof Lab and Texture Bar , guests explored textures, tried products, and spoke with Estheticians about their skin type. With Vaseline Original jellies, oils and lotions on deck, there was something for everyone and every skincare need. Dove extended that attention to underarm and body care through its Advanced Care range, exfoliating scrubs and Beauty Bar. Visitors explored the products and discussed how to give the skin beyond their face the same thoughtful attention. Event-exclusive discounts gave guests another reason to explore. Those who found a product they liked bought it at a discounted rate and received freebies, giving them more opportunities to add healthy skincare to their daily routine. But it was not all skincare. Adding excitement to the shopping and discovery experience, the Vaseline Glow Cam let guests strike a pose and smile for an instant Polaroid. Guests and creators stepped in to capture their best glow. Friends posed together, strangers shared a hello on camera, solo shots turned into mini photoshoots, and the space quickly became one of those BITML stops everyone wanted to experience. Vaseline and Dove’s experience at BITML 2026 reflect how the beauty industry is changing. With social media constantly introducing consumers to new ingredients, routines, and products, there is no shortage of beauty advice to scroll through. But more information brings more questions. Consumers today want to know what a product does, how it feels, whether it suits their skin and whether it can deliver real benefit. At BITML, both brands made everyday care approachable, giving guests opportunities to learn while enjoying the experience. From the Skin Proof Lab to the Texture Bar, expert consultations, and the Glow Cam, Vaseline and Dove showed that skincare d

item.title: SpaceX thrusters just made a Tesla Roadster 'fly' (and Elon Musk's car is still out there in space)
item.description: null Well, that was a memorable debut. Tesla unveiled its highly anticipated new Roadster last night (Oct. 16) with a spectacular stunt, using SpaceX thrusters to make the vehicle "fly." "This is not necessarily a safety-optimized car, OK?" Elon Musk , who runs both companies, said during the livestreamed reveal, which was held at SpaceX's rocket-testing facility in McGregor, Texas. "But it takes the the fun meter to 11 out of 10." Tesla's next-gen, thruster-equipped Roadster launches itself over other vehicles during an unveiling event on Oct. 15, 2026. (Image credit: Tesla) Tesla first announced the next-gen Roadster in 2017, saying at the time that it would be released in 2020 . In 2018, Musk announced that the new car would incorporate some SpaceX tech. "SpaceX option package for new Tesla Roadster will include ~10 small rocket thrusters arranged seamlessly around car. These rocket engines dramatically improve acceleration, top speed, braking & cornering. Maybe they will even allow a Tesla to fly…" he wrote on Twitter in June of that year . (In 2022, Musk bought Twitter , which he subsequently renamed X.) So last night's demonstration didn't come entirely out of left field — but it was still eye-popping. The show began with the Roadster driving up a ramp that quickly became a vertical wall and then an overhanging ledge. The Roadster clung to the surface, hanging upside-down from the ledge like a gecko on a ceiling thanks to a special fan suction system on its chassis. "I mean, this car really sucks, OK?" Musk said, channeling his inner stand-up comedian. "This car could suck the chrome off a trailer hitch. It could suck a tennis ball through a hose pipe." The suction feature is not just a novelty, he added: It will help the Roadster stay connected to the ground during high-speed turns, allowing drivers to corner incredibly well. The next-gen Roadster comes in for a thruster-aided landing during its unveiling event. (Image credit: Tesla) And the sucking was just an opening act. The Tesla soon launched itself from its position beneath the ramp's nearly horizontal ledge, executed a barrel roll in midair, and landed softly, all thanks to its SpaceX cold-gas thrusters. "A friend of mine, Peter Thiel, once said that the future promised us flying cars, but instead we got 140 characters," Musk said after the Roadster touched down. "Well, not anymore." The car has main thrusters in the rear, he explained, as well as attitude-control thrusters that control its orientation. "So it can basically fly like a rocket, and it could do rolls," Musk said. "It could do, like, crazy gymnastics — whatever you want, really." The Roadster has a total of 10 thrusters, which are fed by 600 liters — about 250 kilograms (550 pounds) — of compressed air, Tesla Engineering Vice President Lars Moravy said during last night's event. In 2018, Musk announced that the new car would incorporate some SpaceX tech. "SpaceX option package for new Tesla Roadster will include ~10 small rocket thrusters arranged seamlessly around car. These rocket engines dramatically improve acceleration, top speed, braking & cornering. Maybe they will even allow a Tesla to fly…" he wrote on Twitter in June of that year . (In 2022, Musk bought Twitter , which he subsequently renamed X.) So last night's demonstration didn't come entirely out of left field — but it was still eye-popping. The Roadster clung to the surface, hanging upside-down from the ledge like a gecko on a ceiling thanks to a special fan suction system on its chassis. "I mean, this car really sucks, OK?" Musk said, channeling his inner stand-up comedian. "This car could suck the chrome off a trailer hitch. It could suck a tennis ball through a hose pipe." The suction feature is not just a novelty, he added: It will help the Roadster stay connected to the ground during high-speed turns, allowing drivers to corner incredibly well. The next-gen Roadster comes in for a thruster-aided landing during its unveiling event. (Image credit: Tesla) And the sucking was just an opening act. The Tesla soon launched itself from its position beneath the ramp's nearly horizontal ledge, executed a barrel roll in midair, and landed softly, all thanks to its SpaceX cold-gas thrusters. "A friend of mine, Peter Thiel, once said that the future promised us flying cars, but instead we got 140 characters," Musk said after the Roadster touched down. "Well, not anymore." The car has main thrusters in the rear, he explained, as well as attitude-control thrusters that control its orientation. "So it can basically fly like a rocket, and it could do rolls," Musk said. "It could do, like, crazy gymnastics — whatever you want, really." The Roadster has a total of 10 thrusters, which are fed by 600 liters — about 250 kilograms (550 pounds) — of compressed air, Tesla Engineering Vice President Lars Moravy said during last night's event. That air is housed in carbon fiber overwrapped pressure vessels, which fill "every usable void in the car," Tesla said via X last night. The Tesla team put those thrusters to work multiple times during the presentation, at one point launching the Roadster over a line of six vehicles, including a Tesla semi-truck cab. Nobody was behind the wheel during these stunts — nobody with a pulse, anyway. The driver's seat was occupied by a mannequin clad in a black-and-white SpaceX spacesuit. This was a nod to " Starman ," the dummy behind the wheel of Musk's cherry-red first-gen Roadster, which launched into orbit around the sun in February 2018 on the first-ever flight of SpaceX's Falcon Heavy rocket. Starman and his Roadster are still in space, by the way, and will be for a while. Modeling work suggests the duo will keep orbiting our star for millions of years before ultimately slamming into either Earth or Venus . SpaceX's Starman mannequin sits inside Elon Musk's red Tesla Roadster with Earth in the background, shortly after the initial launch of SpaceX’s Falcon Heavy rocket on Feb. 6, 2018. (Image credit: SpaceX) Last night's Roadster demo was something of a tease, for the car is not yet in showrooms. Musk said Tesla aims to begin producing it in 2028. And don't expect to see the "flying" version on the road then, or anytime; it's hard to imagine regulators certifying that vehicle for everyday use. It will likely be a status symbol for a few wealthy and connected folks, locked away in spacious and well-appointed garages. Indeed, you can't put down on a deposit for the "Rocket" version of the new Roadster on Tesla's website ; purchase of that vehicle is by invite only. Two other Roadster versions are for sale — "Performance" and "Thrust." Tesla's website describes the Performance variant as "road ready," with "active aero and a multi-mode suction system." Thrust, by contrast, is "race ready." It has active aero and suction "plus acceleration thrusters." It costs $50,000 to reserve a Performance vehicle and $250,000 to reserve a Thrust. Tesla has not yet revealed the total cost of any of the new Roadster variants.

item.title: On this day in space! Oct. 16, 1975: NASA launches the 1st-ever GOES weather satellite to watch Earth from space
item.description: null On Oct. 16, 1975, NASA launched the first operational GOES satellite! GOES-A was the first in a series of weather satellites that NASA jointly operated with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). The name is short for Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite . GOES-A launched on a Delta rocket from Cape Canaveral, Florida. GOES satellites all have a geostationary orbit, which means they always face the same part of Earth — in this case, the Indian Ocean. Once GOES-A became operational, it was renamed GOES-1. The GOES satellite fleet has grown over the years, and is a critical link in the chain of satellites tracking Earth's weather from space. In 2016, NASA and NOAA launched GOES-R , the first in a new next-generation series of GOES weather satellites, with more to follow in ensuing years. An artist's illustration of the GOES-1 weather satellite. (Image credit: NOAA) Why it mattered With weather forecasts so prevalent (you can literally find them in the palm of your hand with a smartphone), it may be hard to think that such daily information wasn't always readily available. But that was the case when NOAA began building what has become an essential part of the U.S. weather monitoring fleet of satellites . GOES-A, or GOES-1 as it was later called, "gave forecasters their first near-real time look at atmospheric conditions from a fixed location," NOAA officials said in an overview . The satellite launched from Pad 17A at what is now the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station and returned its first photo just nine days after liftoff, on Oct. 25, 1975. The satellite was equipped with a Visible/Infrared Spin Scan Radiometer (VISSR) to capture Earth observations in daylight and nighttime to track clouds and surface temperature. The spin-stabilized satellite was able to observe Earth just 10% of the time, but was still the most up-to-date satellite observations for weather forecasters . GOES-1 was active until March 7, 1985, when it was ultimately decommissioned. But during that time, NASA and NOAA launched five more successors, GOES 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. "For 50 years, GOES data has been the backbone of short-term forecasts and warnings of severe weather and environmental hazards in the Western Hemisphere and forecasts and warnings of space weather hazards," NOAA wrote while celebrating 50 years of GOES satellites. "Each successive generation of GOES has brought improvements and new capabilities to monitor our part of the world." Since the first next-generation GOES satellite, GOES-R, launched in 2016, NOAA has flown another three satellites, most recently with GOES-U weather satellite launch in 2024. Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.

item.title: Understanding Your Milk Options: A Dietitian’s Guide to Choosing the Right Milk
item.description: Buying milk used to be simple; you walked into a supermarket, reached for a familiar tin or sachet, and carried on with the rest of your shopping. Today, that same trip can leave many people standing in the dairy aisle far longer than they expected. While shopping at one of the large supermarkets when a young couple standing in front of the milk shelf was noticed. They had been there for what felt like ten minutes, carefully picking up one product after another, turning the packs over to read the labels before placing them back. The wife was scrolling through Instagram, almost desperately, as though she hoped someone had recently posted the answer to the question they were trying to solve. “ Which milk should we buy?” Interestingly, they weren’t comparing brands or prices. They were trying to understand the different options available. Should they choose dairy milk or a non-dairy alternative? And if dairy was the right choice, what exactly was the difference between Full Cream Milk and Filled Milk ? They wanted to make the right choice but weren’t sure what those terms meant. Eventually, I smiled and walked over. “ Hello, I’m sorry to interrupt. I’m a dietitian, and from what I’ve overheard, I think I can help explain the differences.” Within a few minutes, what had seemed like a complicated shopping decision suddenly became much clearer. They thanked me, picked the product that best suited what they were looking for and continued with the rest of their shopping. That encounter reminded me of something I have observed repeatedly throughout my years of practice: many consumers assume that milk is simply… milk. Yet today’s supermarket shelves tell a very different story. Before deciding which milk to buy, many consumers are first faced with an important question: Should I choose dairy milk or a non-dairy alternative? For those who choose dairy milk, there is another decision to make. Understanding the difference between Full Cream Milk, Filled Milk and age-appropriate milk products is key to choosing the option that best meets their needs. The challenge is that these differences aren’t always obvious to the average shopper. As a result, many people make their decisions based on familiarity, price or attractive packaging rather than understanding what the product was designed to do. Making informed food choices doesn’t always begin with eating something different. Sometimes, it begins with simply understanding what you’re buying. And that’s exactly where we’ll begin. Eventually, I smiled and walked over. “ Hello, I’m sorry to interrupt. I’m a dietitian, and from what I’ve overheard, I think I can help explain the differences.” Within a few minutes, what had seemed like a complicated shopping decision suddenly became much clearer. They thanked me, picked the product that best suited what they were looking for and continued with the rest of their shopping. That encounter reminded me of something I have observed repeatedly throughout my years of practice: many consumers assume that milk is simply… milk. Yet today’s supermarket shelves tell a very different story. Before deciding which milk to buy, many consumers are first faced with an important question: Should I choose dairy milk or a non-dairy alternative? For those who choose dairy milk, there is another decision to make. Understanding the difference between Full Cream Milk, Filled Milk and age-appropriate milk products is key to choosing the option that best meets their needs. The challenge is that these differences aren’t always obvious to the average shopper. As a result, many people make their decisions based on familiarity, price or attractive packaging rather than understanding what the product was designed to do. Making informed food choices doesn’t always begin with eating something different. Sometimes, it begins with simply understanding what you’re buying. And that’s exactly where we’ll begin. Understanding the Two Main Milk Options When we think about the milk aisle, it can sometimes feel as though there are endless options. The first decision is much simpler than many people realise. Broadly speaking, there is Dairy milk and non-dairy milk Dairy milk comes from animals, most commonly cows, although goat’s and sheep’s milk are also consumed in many parts of the world. It naturally provides high-quality protein, calcium and several essential vitamins and minerals that support growth, bone health and overall wellbeing. For consumers who choose dairy milk, there is one more decision to make. Not All Dairy Milk Products Are The Same Within the dairy category, the two most common options consumers will come across are Full Cream Milk and Filled Milk. While both are dairy products and both provide important nutrients, they differ in their fat composition and are designed to meet different nutritional needs and consumer preferences. Understanding these differences is the next step in choosing the milk that’s right for you. Understanding Your Options Standing in that supermarket, I realised the couple weren’t just trying to choose a brand. They were trying to understand which type of dairy milk best suited their needs. Once you’ve decided that dairy milk is the right choice for you, the next step is understanding the different dairy products available. Peak’s dairy range, for example, includes Full Cream Milk, Filled Milk and Peak 456 Growing-Up Milk . Although they all contain dairy ingredients, each has been developed to meet different nutritional needs and life stages. Rather than thinking of these as different versions of the same product, it helps to think of each one as serving a different purpose. Peak Full Cream Milk is designed to provide complete dairy nutrition for everyday family use. Peak Filled Milk, on the other hand, offers consumers another dairy option with a different fat composition while still providing important nutrients such as protein and calcium. Peak 456 Growing-Up Milk is specially formulated to support the nutritional needs of children aged four to six years. Understanding what each product is designed to do makes choosing the right one much easier. Let’s take a closer look at each one. Peak Full Cream Milk When most people think of milk, Full Cream Milk is usually what comes to mind. Made from whole cow’s milk, it naturally contains milk fat, giving it the rich, creamy taste many people enjoy. It also provides complete dairy nutrition by supplying high-quality protein, calcium and a range of essential vitamins and minerals that contribute to bone health, muscle function and overall wellbeing. One example within this category is Peak Full Cream Milk, which is available in both powdered and evaporated formats. Its versatility makes it suitable for drinking, breakfast cereals, smoothies, tea, coffee, cooking and baking, making it a practical choice for everyday family use. Best suited for: Families looking for complete dairy nutrition for everyday use. Peak Filled Milk Filled Milk is a dairy milk product in which part or all the natural milk fat has been replaced with vegetable oils. While this gives it a different fat composition from Full Cream Milk, it continues to provide important nutrients such as high-quality protein, calcium and essential vitamins. Peak Filled Milk offers consumers another dairy milk option that combines these nutritional benefits with a different fat composition to suit varying dietary preferences. Rather than thinking of Filled Milk as “better” or “worse” than Full Cream Milk, it is more helpful to understand that each product has been developed to meet different consumer needs. The right choice depends on your nutritional requirements, health goals and personal preferences. Best suited for: Consumers looking for a dairy milk option with a different fat composition. Peak 456 Growing-Up Milk Children have different nutritional needs at different stages of growth, which is why age-appropriate milk products have an important role in supporting a balanced diet. Peak 456 Growing-Up Milk is specially formulated for children aged four to six years. In addition to providing high-quality protein and calcium, it is fortified with essential vitamins and DHA, an omega-3 fatty acid that supports normal brain development during childhood. By providing nutrients tailored to this stage of growth, Peak 456 helps support the nutritional needs of young children as part of a healthy, balanced diet. Best suited for: Children aged 4–6 years. A Simple Guide to Choosing the Right Milk Choosing the right milk doesn’t have to be complicated. Once you understand what each product is designed to do, the decision becomes much simpler. If you’re looking for… A suitable option is… Complete dairy nutrition for the family Peak Full Cream Milk A dairy milk option with a different fat composition Peak Filled Milk Nutrition designed for children aged 4–6 years Peak 456 Growing-Up Milk Before adding any dairy milk product to your shopping basket, ask yourself three simple questions: Which dairy milk do I need? Full Cream or Filled milk Who am I buying this product for? Does this product meet my nutritional needs and suit how I intend to use it? Answering these questions can help you move beyond attractive packaging or familiarity and choose the product that best suits your needs and those of your family. Choosing

item.title: 'Dark Matter's' Joel Edgerton and Jennifer Connelly talk S2's marital disintegration and the humility of hanging on wires (interview)
item.description: null The eighth episode of Apple TV's "Dark Matter" season 2 has just dropped, and we're all on the edge of our seats trying to guess how the strange saga of Jason (Joel Edgerton) and Daniela (Jennifer Connelly) Dessen is going to finish up. Not even fans of the books know, as this superb adaptation of NYT bestselling author Blake Crouch's 2016 novel broke out of its source material for season 2. For Edgerton and Connelly, "Dark Matter" has been a whirlwind project as their characters search for a safe alternate universe while being pursued by a multiplicity of Jasons. The physical rigors and emotional toll of shooting the show and presenting its nuanced storytelling often proved difficult. "There's two exhaustions that I’ve found in movie work," Edgerton tells Space. "It's either mental exhaustion from going to dark emotional places in your brain or complex dialogue stuff. Then there's the physical challenges, like for doing a fight scene. One of the weirdest ones on 'Dark Matter' was doing a gravity scene where we’re dangling on wires inside The Box. There's something deeply exhausting about it and a bit humiliating. You feel like a human teabag." Joel Edgerton and Dayo Okeniyi star in Apple TV's "Dark Matter" season 2 (Image credit: Apple TV) Connelly was also a part of that tough sequence and reflects on Edgerton’s tireless fortitude. "Joel's schedule on this show is really brutal," she notes. "He's in almost all of it. This season is better, but season 1 was crazy for him. It’s surprising; sometimes the things that are most difficult are the ones you don’t anticipate. That's more exhausting at the end of the day after trying to get something to work that you didn’t think would be tricky. I like the days that are tiring because you feel drained because you’ve explored a lot in a scene. That's a nice feeling." For Edgerton, the simplest thing to remember is that when practicing your craft, always make sure that you go home each day feeling satisfied with what you shot. "There's nothing worse than going home and thinking that you didn’t get the best out of yourself," he reveals. "As they say, as actors we're not digging trenches. It's not hard physical labor; it's a different kind of thing. Until actually I shot a movie where I had to dig a trench." Working with Blake Crouch on the series and its unnerving portrait of a marriage strewn across the infinite multiverse has produced new insights into their own lives. "I find there’s something to be learned from each experience as an actor," notes Edgerton. "Each story takes you through something, whether you like to think it or not. "You either learn a skill or meet an actor that you admire, and they teach you something inspired by their presence. We were tasked with helping Blake build the disintegration of a marriage, and it's the opposite of what you’re hoping for in real life. That each day you hope you're turning up contributing in a positive way to your relationship rather than engineering it

Then there's the physical challenges, like for doing a fight scene. One of the weirdest ones on 'Dark Matter' was doing a gravity scene where we’re dangling on wires inside The Box. There's something deeply exhausting about it and a bit humiliating. You feel like a human teabag." Joel Edgerton and Dayo Okeniyi star in Apple TV's "Dark Matter" season 2 (Image credit: Apple TV) Connelly was also a part of that tough sequence and reflects on Edgerton’s tireless fortitude. "Joel's schedule on this show is really brutal," she notes. "He's in almost all of it. This season is better, but season 1 was crazy for him. I like the days that are tiring because you feel drained because you’ve explored a lot in a scene. That's a nice feeling." For Edgerton, the simplest thing to remember is that when practicing your craft, always make sure that you go home each day feeling satisfied with what you shot. It's not hard physical labor; it's a different kind of thing. Until actually I shot a movie where I had to dig a trench." Working with Blake Crouch on the series and its unnerving portrait of a marriage strewn across the infinite multiverse has produced new insights into their own lives. "I find there’s something to be learned from each experience as an actor," notes Edgerton. "Each story takes you through something, whether you like to think it or not. "You either learn a skill or meet an actor that you admire, and they teach you something inspired by their presence. We were tasked with helping Blake build the disintegration of a marriage, and it's the opposite of what you’re hoping for in real life. That each day you hope you're turning up contributing in a positive way to your relationship rather than engineering its demise. It makes you think about how you can be a better person in life. And there's always room for improvement." Jennifer Connelly and Joel Edgerton are treating fans to an extraordinary trip in "Dark Matter" season 2 (Image credit: Apple TV) Likewise, Connelly sees a sort of emotional mirroring effect to be absorbed that extends beyond "Dark Matter's" detailed sets, dizzying locations, and sound stages. "I think Daniela, at a point when Jason is going down paths, and they're struggling, recognizes that sometimes it's hard to distinguish what is really the other person and what we’re bringing to our perception of them," she adds. "She has things in her history that bias her vision, and she takes herself off on a journey to reconcile those things and try to take responsibility for healing. And that's a good lesson to remember in relationships in general. Being on top of one's own part of the dynamic. Sometimes things we see in each other are really things within ourselves." "Dark Matter" season 2 airs each Friday exclusively on Apple TV, with the season finale (and perhaps the series end if not renewed) arriving on Oct. 30, 2026. Watch Dark Matter on Apple TV+: Apple TV+: $12.99/month (7-day free trial) Apple TV & Peacock Premium: $14.99/month

item.title: 'Mission: 60s' event promises passport back to the Space Age
item.description: null Your invitation to revisit the Space Age has arrived. Whether you miss the days when people got dressed up to fly or you wish your "other" ride was a rocket , Mission: 60s has a *space* reserved for you. "This is a three-day celebration of Apollo , aviation, space exploration and 1960s culture," reads a promo for the Oct. 23 to 25 event in New York. "You will be fully immersed in the sights, sounds and spirit of the 1960s Space Age." "The weekend features astronauts, Apollo flight directors, Mission Control engineers, Star Trek legends, space artists, a Saturday Spacefarer Soiree with live music (1960s attire encouraged!), and a Sunday NASA Artemis keynote." Organized by Luna Replicas, a company specializing in vintage space gear, and Space for Humanity, a nonprofit that underwrites spaceflight experiences, Mission: 60s is aimed at being the bridge between the last time humanity reached for the moon and today's " second space race " to do it again — this time to stay. Mission: 60s at the TWA Hotel, Oct. 23-25, 2026, includes a tour of the 1964 World's Fair site and its NASA Apollo-era rocket displays. (Image credit: Mission 60s) Launch pad Your journey back to the 60s begins when you check into the TWA Hotel at the John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) in New York. Once a functioning terminal for Trans World Airlines (as featured in the 2002 movie "Catch Me If You Can"), the TWA Flight Center has been reimagined as a hotel like no other. "At the center of the hotel is Eero Saarinen's iconic TWA Flight Center, where restaurants, bars and retail outlets have taken flight. Two hotel wings, designed to reflect and defer to the landmark TWA Flight Center, sit behind the historic building and contain 512 guest rooms with views of JFK's runways and the TWA Flight Center," reads the hotel's website . The TWA Hotel is only the first sight straight out of the past that guests will encounter. On Friday (Oct. 23), Mission: 60s begins with a guided tour of the 1964 World's Fair site in Flushing Meadows. Today the home to the New York Hall of Science, the outdoor exhibits includes the Rocket Park, where Gemini-Titan II and Mercury-Atlas D rockets and a Saturn V F-1 engine still stand. "The space age was less than 10 years old when rockets like these powered incredible missions to outer space," reads the description on the museum's website. "Visitors will learn about the history of these vehicles as well as the United States' mission to reach the moon." Also on view at the World's Fair site is the Unisphere, a spherical stainless steel representation of Earth , and the Astro-View Observation Towers (later reimagined as actual flying saucers in the 1997 movie "Men in Black"). The first day concludes with Space For Humanity's (separately-ticketed) " Celestial Soiree " and a Mission: 60's pool party on the hotel's rooftop. Two hotel wings, designed to reflect and defer to the landmark TWA Flight Center, sit behind the historic building and contain 512 guest rooms with views of JFK's runways and the TWA Flight Center," reads the hotel's website . The TWA Hotel is only the first sight straight out of the past that guests will encounter. "The space age was less than 10 years old when rockets like these powered incredible missions to outer space," reads the description on the museum's website. "Visitors will learn about the history of these vehicles as well as the United States' mission to reach the moon." Also on view at the World's Fair site is the Unisphere, a spherical stainless steel representation of Earth , and the Astro-View Observation Towers (later reimagined as actual flying saucers in the 1997 movie "Men in Black"). The first day concludes with Space For Humanity's (separately-ticketed) " Celestial Soiree " and a Mission: 60's pool party on the hotel's rooftop. MCC, ILC and ILM Saturday and Sunday at Mission: 60s will bring together members of Mission Control (MCC), spaceflight experts (including ILC Dover, makers of the Apollo spacesuit ) and representatives from the Hollywood community who brought about the 60s-era visions of space exploration (including Industrial Light & Magic [ILM]) for a series of engaging panel discussions. Among the various topics scheduled for the two days of talks are: Apollo Mission Control & Flight Operations Apollo to Artemis & Beyond Women in Aerospace Apollo Communications: The Sights & Sounds From the Moon SciFi Inspires The Overview Effect Making Space Real: Art & Visual Effects That Sold Humanity on Space Space Advocacy Mission: 60s includes two full days of discussion panels spanning topics such as the Apollo spacesuit to the role of sci-fi in inspiring space exploration. (Image credit: Mission 60s) Featured speakers and moderators include Apollo flight director Gerry Griffin, TIME Magazine science editor Jeffrey Kluger, former NASA astronauts Nicole Stott and Ron Garan, "Star Trek" actor Bob Picardo and researcher Frank White. On Saturday evening, there will be a second gala, "The Spacefarer Soiree," featuring a limited meet and greet aboard a Lockheed Constellation airliner and music by Bonnie Gordon. Set in 1969, attendees are encouraged to come wearing their finest period clothing. Then, on Sunday afternoon, Uplift Aerospace will host a shared "Overview" VR experience for up to 50 people participating together. Both days will include a vendor and artists' hall, with guests signing autographs and their books, as well as companies such as NASA's official patch provider A-B Emblem, selling Apollo-themed souvenirs and memorabilia. A weekend pass is $150 per person, with add-ons for VIP access, the galas and Friday's World Fair excursion. Single-day admission is $85.

item.title: Why can you see the moon during the day? This week is the perfect time to find out
item.description: null I know perfectly well that the moon comes out during the day. I have known this for decades. Yet whenever I spot it in a blue afternoon sky, some primitive part of my brain still thinks it has turned up early. I'm certainly not the only one. Many people don't understand how it could be visible in daylight. In their eyes, the moon is a nighttime object. Why? Because that's when they notice it — it appears brighter. We tend to think of the sun as belonging to the day and the moon to the night because that's how they're usually presented to us as children. Astronomically, it makes little sense. The moon spends plenty of time above our horizon while the sun is also up — it spends half its time in the daytime sky, in fact. If the moon, pale but unmistakable, looks slightly out of place against a blue sky , it's not — you are. This week is a great time to get used to seeing it there. Just past first quarter, the moon will spend each afternoon hanging in the daytime sky, becoming easier to spot as the sun sinks towards the horizon. What's happening and when to look The moon reached first quarter on Sunday, Oct. 18, and is now waxing toward full moon, which occurs early on Monday, Oct. 26 (Oct. 25 in some time zones). That puts it in the right part of its orbit to be conspicuous during the late afternoon this weekend. Here's the useful bit to remember. Around first quarter, the moon rises roughly around midday. As it waxes towards full, it rises progressively later in the afternoon. By full moon, it rises around sunset. The moon reached first quarter on Oct. 18. (Image credit: Taro Hama @ e-kamakura via Getty Images) That makes the days immediately after first quarter an excellent time to get into the habit of finding the moon before sunset. On Monday, Oct. 19, look southeast in the afternoon for a moon just over half-lit. Each afternoon this week, it will become a little more illuminated, move farther east against the background stars, and appear progressively later in the day. You don't need to wait until dusk. In fact, that's the point. Start looking during the afternoon, when the sun is still well above the horizon. Once you find the moon, it can be surprisingly conspicuous against the blue sky. item.content:encoded: null I know perfectly well that the moon comes out during the day. I have known this for decades. Yet whenever I spot it in a blue afternoon sky, some primitive part of my brain still thinks it has turned up early. I'm certainly not the only one. Many people don't understand how it could be visible in daylight. In their eyes, the moon is a nighttime object. Why? Because that's when they notice it — it appears brighter. We tend to think of the sun as belonging to the day and the moon to the night because that's how they're usually presented to us as children. Astronomically, it makes little sense. The moon spends plenty of time above our horizon while the sun is also up — it spends half its time in the daytime sky, in fact. If the moon, pale but unmistakable, looks slightly out of place against a blue sky , it's not — you are. This week is a great time to get used to seeing it there. Just past first quarter, the moon will spend each afternoon hanging in the daytime sky, becoming easier to spot as the sun sinks towards the horizon. What's happening and when to look The moon reached first quarter on Sunday, Oct. 18, and is now waxing toward full moon, which occurs early on Monday, Oct. 26 (Oct. 25 in some time zones). That puts it in the right part of its orbit to be conspicuous during the late afternoon this weekend. Here's the useful bit to remember. Around first quarter, the moon rises roughly around midday. As it waxes towards full, it rises progressively later in the afternoon. By full moon, it rises around sunset. The moon reached first quarter on Oct. 18. (Image credit: Taro Hama @ e-kamakura via Getty Images) That makes the days immediately after first quarter an excellent time to get into the habit of finding the moon before sunset. On Monday, Oct. 19, look southeast in the afternoon for a moon just over half-lit. Each afternoon this week, it will become a little more illuminated, move farther east against the background stars, and appear progressively later in the day. You don't need to wait until dusk. In fact, that's the point. Start looking during the afternoon, when the sun is still well above the horizon. Once you find the moon, it can be surprisingly conspicuous against the blue sky. How and when I'm watching it The moon is now waxing towards being full, so it's already in the sky by dusk. (Image credit: 5c5q2cnvmg / 500px via Getty Images) I'll start looking in the mid-to-late afternoon this week, when the waxing moon should already be high enough to find easily. You can check the exact moonrise time where you are , but there's no need to catch it as it rises. Look towards the east or southeast and scan the blue sky. Once you've found the moon in daylight, keep checking on it as sunset approaches. The moon doesn't suddenly become brighter, of course. Instead, the surrounding sky darkens, increasing the contrast until the pale daytime moon seems to switch on at dusk and grow increasingly brilliant. Binoculars will give you a superb view at dusk, particularly along the terminator — the boundary between lunar day and night. That's where low-angle sunlight throws mountains and crater rims into sharp relief. As the moon waxes this week, the terminator will move steadily across its surface, revealing a different landscape each afternoon. That's another reason not to wait for the full moon. The full moon gets most of the attention, but the week beforehand is arguably a much better time to get to know our nearest celestial neighbor — and you don't even have to wait until dark. Stargazer's corner: October 23-29, 2026 The full moon arrives on Monday, Oct. 26. (Image credit: Westend61 via Getty Images) This is a bright-moon week. Full moon arrives early on Monday, Oct. 26, so moonlight will wash out faint stars and make galaxies and nebulas much harder to see. So go for Saturn instead. It reached opposition earlier this month and remains very well placed in the evening sky. Better still, the nearly full moon passes near Saturn around Oct. 23-24, giving beginners a convenient landmark for locating the planet. The moon's glare will hide faint nearby stars, but Saturn itself is easily bright enough to cope. A good example will be Oct. 27, when the Pleiades is passed closely by a bright moon. The Seven Sisters therefore won't be at their best, so you'll need to use binoculars — if you do, you'll see them easily enough. Constellation of the week: Auriga Auriga is one of the easiest constellations to find in the Northern Hemisphere's winter night sky. (Image credit: E. Slawik/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/M. Zamani) Auriga, "the Charioteer," is climbing in the northeastern and eastern sky during late October evenings. It's easiest to find if you start at Capella, one of the brightest stars in the entire night sky. It's just 43 light-years from the sun. From there, I look for the other stars that form Auriga's rough pentagon, including Menkalinan, Mahasim and Almaaz. The fifth corner is Elnath, although it officially belongs to neighboring Taurus . Auriga gets even better with binoculars. The Milky Way runs straight through it, bringing with it three bright open star clusters — M36, M37 and M38. All three show up in binoculars under a reasonably dark sky, while a small telescope starts to resolve them into individual stars. There's always another layer to find in the night sky. My latest stargazing obsession There's something special about stargazing during the blue hour — that brief transition when daylight drains from the sky and night's window begins to open. It's particularly beautiful a few days before full moon, when the near-full orb is already rising in the east as the sun sets in the west. Look below it, and you may also see the Belt of Venus, a pinkish band above the eastern horizon caused by reddened sunlight shining through Earth's atmosphere , with our planet's dark blue-gray shadow beneath. As the sky fades through ever-deeper shades of blue, the moon brightens, and the first stars emerge around it.

item.title: 7 best places to see the northern lights, according to an aurora chaser
item.description: null I've spent years chasing the northern lights across the Arctic, from the mountains of Swedish Lapland to the dramatic Norwegian fjords. If there's one thing I've learned, it's that choosing where to see the northern lights is about much more than simply heading as far north as possible. Whether you're on the hunt for somewhere that offers the best chance of clear skies, the most dramatic scenery or a plethora of winter activities to keep you warm, choosing the right destination can make a big difference, especially as auroras are never guaranteed. My biggest piece of advice? Choose somewhere you've always wanted to visit regardless of whether the northern lights might appear. That way, the auroras become the icing on the cake rather than the sole measure of a successful trip. From my personal favorites in Scandinavia to some of North America's most established aurora hotspots, here are seven of the best places to see the northern lights this 2026/27 season. Best places to see the northern lights at a glance Best places to see the northern lights at a glance Location Best for Kiruna and Abisko, Sweden Best for a short northern lights trip Tromsø, Norway Best for a city break Norwegian coast Best for a scenic Arctic voyage Finnish Lapland Best for a winter wonderland getaway Iceland Best for volcanoes, glaciers and natural wonders Fairbanks, Alaska Best for a U.S. aurora getaway Yellowknife, Canada Best for a Canadian aurora getaway Abisko and Kiruna, Sweden: Best for a short northern lights trip Northern lights from Mount Nuolja, Abisko, Sweden. (Image credit: Daisy Dobrijevic) Best time to visit: September to early April Swedish Lapland holds a particularly special place in my heart. It's where I saw the northern lights for the very first time, during a trip to Kiruna in February 2023. I'd only booked two nights in Kiruna, one of which included a northern lights tour with Anders from Outdoor North 67º . Talk about putting all your eggs in one basket! But the gamble paid off, and I was treated to a spellbinding display of auroras dancing across the Arctic sky. I've been hooked ever since. Kiruna offers a wide range of accommodation, restaurants and activities, making it a convenient base for exploring the region. From here, you can join guided aurora tours, visit the famous Icehotel in Jukkasjärvi or head into the wilderness for dog sledding and snowmobiling adventures. One of the region's biggest draws is Abisko National Park, around 60 miles (100 kilometers) northwest of Kiruna. Abisko is famous for its so-called "Blue Hole" , a local weather phenomenon in which the skies above the national park can be clear, even if the surrounding region (and weather forecast) is cloudy. item.dc:creator: Daisy Dobrijevic
item.content:encoded: null I've spent years chasing the northern lights across the Arctic, from the mountains of Swedish Lapland to the dramatic Norwegian fjords. If there's one thing I've learned, it's that choosing where to see the northern lights is about much more than simply heading as far north as possible. Whether you're on the hunt for somewhere that offers the best chance of clear skies, the most dramatic scenery or a plethora of winter activities to keep you warm, choosing the right destination can make a big difference, especially as auroras are never guaranteed. My biggest piece of advice? Choose somewhere you've always wanted to visit regardless of whether the northern lights might appear. That way, the auroras become the icing on the cake rather than the sole measure of a successful trip. From my personal favorites in Scandinavia to some of North America's most established aurora hotspots, here are seven of the best places to see the northern lights this 2026/27 season. Best places to see the northern lights at a glance Best places to see the northern lights at a glance Location Best for Kiruna and Abisko, Sweden Best for a short northern lights trip Tromsø, Norway Best for a city break Norwegian coast Best for a scenic Arctic voyage Finnish Lapland Best for a winter wonderland getaway Iceland Best for volcanoes, glaciers and natural wonders Fairbanks, Alaska Best for a U.S. aurora getaway Yellowknife, Canada Best for a Canadian aurora getaway Abisko and Kiruna, Sweden: Best for a short northern lights trip Northern lights from Mount Nuolja, Abisko, Sweden. (Image credit: Daisy Dobrijevic) Best time to visit: September to early April Swedish Lapland holds a particularly special place in my heart. It's where I saw the northern lights for the very first time, during a trip to Kiruna in February 2023. I'd only booked two nights in Kiruna, one of which included a northern lights tour with Anders from Outdoor North 67º . Talk about putting all your eggs in one basket! But the gamble paid off, and I was treated to a spellbinding display of auroras dancing across the Arctic sky. I've been hooked ever since. Kiruna offers a wide range of accommodation, restaurants and activities, making it a convenient base for exploring the region. From here, you can join guided aurora tours, visit the famous Icehotel in Jukkasjärvi or head into the wilderness for dog sledding and snowmobiling adventures. One of the region's biggest draws is Abisko National Park, around 60 miles (100 kilometers) northwest of Kiruna. Abisko is famous for its so-called "Blue Hole" , a local weather phenomenon in which the skies above the national park can be clear, even if the surrounding region (and weather forecast) is cloudy. This is partly thanks to the surrounding mountains, which create a rain shadow effect, reducing the precipitation in the area. Glacial-carved valley Lapporten, in Abisko National Park. (Image credit: Daisy Dobrijevic) And if you're visiting Abisko, I'd highly recommend taking the chairlift up Mount Nuolja to the Aurora Sky Station . The views across Abisko National Park and the surrounding mountains are spectacular. Just be sure to check the chairlift's operating dates and times before visiting, as it doesn't run throughout the entire season. My tip: Although my two-night gamble paid off, I wouldn't recommend relying on such a short window if seeing the northern lights is your main goal. If possible, give yourself at least three or four nights to improve your chances of clear skies and aurora activity. Tromsø, Norway: Best for a city break Tromsø is the perfect destination for an aurora city break. (Image credit: Juan Maria Coy Vergara via Getty Images) Best time to visit: September to early April If you want to experience the northern lights without giving up the comforts of city life, Tromsø is hard to beat. Located high above the Arctic Circle in northern Norway, Tromsø sits beneath the auroral oval, the region surrounding Earth's magnetic poles where auroras occur most frequently. What I particularly like about Tromsø is that it offers the best of both worlds. You have a lively city with excellent restaurants, cafes, shops, museums and accommodation, while spectacular mountains and wilderness are only a short journey away. There's also a huge range of northern lights tours available, from small-group photography excursions to longer aurora-chasing adventures. My tip: Tromsø is ideal if you want to combine northern lights hunting with a city break holiday. I'd recommend booking at least one guided aurora tour, particularly if the local weather forecast looks challenging. The Norwegian coast: Best for a scenic Arctic voyage Northern lights during a cruise along the Norwegian coast with Hurtigruten. (Image credit: Daisy Dobrijevic) Best time to visit: September to March If there's one northern lights experience I'd encourage people to consider, it's sailing along the Norwegian coast. I've been fortunate enough to travel along this extraordinary coastline on several occasions , and there's something very special about watching the northern lights from the deck of a ship, surrounded by good company, mountains, fjords and the dark Arctic sea. Operators such as Hurtigruten and HX offer voyages along the Norwegian coast, combining opportunities to see the northern lights with some of the most spectacular scenery in Europe. While Hurtigruten operates coastal voyages calling at towns and communities along the route, HX offers expedition-style experiences with a focus on exploring the natural environment. Arctic Norway during the winter months offers truly stunning views. Photo captured during a Hurtigruten voyage. (Image credit: Daisy Dobrijevic) Rather than staying in one location, you'll travel through different coastal landscapes, with opportunities to experience Arctic wildlife, local culture and winter excursions along the way. And then, of course, there's the possibility of the northern lights appearing overhead. Join me on a northern lights voyage! (Image credit: Daisy Dobrijevic) I'll be setting sail on a handful of Hurtigruten's astronomy voyages as a guest lecturer, sharing the science and wonder of the northern lights along the way. However, there's an important trade-off. Unlike a land-based aurora chase, a ship can't simply drive inland to escape coastal cloud cover. You're largely dependent on the weather along your route, although traveling through different regions over several nights gives you multiple opportunities. Hurtigruten also offers a Northern Lights Promise on qualifying voyages, providing a complimentary return voyage if the lights aren't officially sighted during your trip. Be sure to check the eligibility requirements and terms before booking. My tip: Choose a Norwegian coastal voyage because you want to experience the coastline itself. The scenery, communities and Arctic landscapes make it a remarkable journey regardless of auroras. Finnish Lapland: Best for a winter wonderland getaway Best time to visit: September to March If you dream of a northern lights holiday involving snow-covered forests, cozy cabins and perhaps even watching auroras from a glass-roofed igloo, Finnish Lapland could be the perfect choice. Northern Finland lies beneath the auroral oval, making it a popular destination for aurora chasers. Places such as Inari, Saariselkä and Ivalo offer excellent access to dark skies and Arctic wilderness. Rovaniemi, the official hometown of Santa Claus, is another popular option, particularly for families, although it's worth traveling away from the city's lights for the best views. My tip: For a quieter, more wilderness-focused escape, I'd look at northern Lapland around Inari or Saariselkä. If you're traveling with children or want a more activity-packed holiday, Rovaniemi may be a better fit. item.title: Beyond pointing your phone at the night sky, this is how to use stargazing apps effectively
item.description: Whether you are a seasoned astronomer or a newcomer to the hobby, the best stargazing apps have the potential to seriously enhance your skywatching experience. But it's easy to overlook just how useful these portable programs can be. That's why we've put together this guide to getting the best use out of stargazing apps, from identifying stars and constellations through to seeking out dark sky sites and beyond. You will wonder how you ever managed without them. So read on and get ready to take your stargazing to the next level. And if you're wondering how else technology can take the work out of skywatching, we've also rounded up the best smart telescopes . Using stargazing apps Some apps use Augmented Reality (AR) features to allow users to scan the sky in real-time. (Image credit: Getty Images) Before we explore specific uses, there are a few things you need to know about using the best stargazing apps on your Apple or Android device. Firstly, while some apps support offline use, you'll typically need a mobile or Wi-Fi signal with data to make the most of these apps. Also, some apps lock certain features behind a paywall. Pay for Stellarium Plus, for example, and you get an additional 2 million deep sky objects, the ability to connect to certain telescopes and more. Finally, while many stargazing apps are relatively intuitive, we'd recommend you familiarize yourself with them at home before taking them out into the field. Identifying stars in the field Sky Tonight is one of the apps that, via AR, can be used to identify stars and other objects. (Image credit: Vito Technology) One of the most common and convenient uses for stargazing apps is identifying stars, constellations and more, just by pointing your phone's camera at them. It really is that simple. Take Sky Tonight , which we think is the best stargazing app for AR (augmented reality). Launch the app, grant it camera access and turn it towards the object you want to identify. The name will appear on screen and you can also tap to learn more about it, whether it's a star, constellation, planet or nebula. Conversely, you can also use the app to find specific objects in the sky. Want to view Uranus at opposition this Nov. 25 but aren't sure where to look? Search for it in Sky Tonight and the app will point you to it. item.dc:creator: Chris McMullen
item.content:encoded: Whether you are a seasoned astronomer or a newcomer to the hobby, the best stargazing apps have the potential to seriously enhance your skywatching experience. But it's easy to overlook just how useful these portable programs can be. That's why we've put together this guide to getting the best use out of stargazing apps, from identifying stars and constellations through to seeking out dark sky sites and beyond. You will wonder how you ever managed without them. So read on and get ready to take your stargazing to the next level. And if you're wondering how else technology can take the work out of skywatching, we've also rounded up the best smart telescopes . Using stargazing apps Some apps use Augmented Reality (AR) features to allow users to scan the sky in real-time. (Image credit: Getty Images) Before we explore specific uses, there are a few things you need to know about using the best stargazing apps on your Apple or Android device. Firstly, while some apps support offline use, you'll typically need a mobile or Wi-Fi signal with data to make the most of these apps. Also, some apps lock certain features behind a paywall. Pay for Stellarium Plus, for example, and you get an additional 2 million deep sky objects, the ability to connect to certain telescopes and more. Finally, while many stargazing apps are relatively intuitive, we'd recommend you familiarize yourself with them at home before taking them out into the field. Identifying stars in the field Sky Tonight is one of the apps that, via AR, can be used to identify stars and other objects. (Image credit: Vito Technology) One of the most common and convenient uses for stargazing apps is identifying stars, constellations and more, just by pointing your phone's camera at them. It really is that simple. Take Sky Tonight , which we think is the best stargazing app for AR (augmented reality). Launch the app, grant it camera access and turn it towards the object you want to identify. The name will appear on screen and you can also tap to learn more about it, whether it's a star, constellation, planet or nebula. Conversely, you can also use the app to find specific objects in the sky. Want to view Uranus at opposition this Nov. 25 but aren't sure where to look? Search for it in Sky Tonight and the app will point you to it. Identifiying stars from photographs Sky Walk 2 lets you rewind and advance time, showing you where stars and other objects were or will be on that date. (Image credit: Future) Being able to identify night sky objects in the field is a real boon, but what if you've already taken a photograph and want to identify which stars were visible? That's where apps like Sky Walk 2 come in. If possible, you should return to the location where the photograph was taken, but if that's not possible, you can input GPS co-ordinates and Sky Walk 2 will show you the view from that location. Next, using the clock icon and slider, alter the date to the exact time you took the photograph (or as near as possible). You will then be shown the night sky as it was at the time. You can now tap on the star or stars you want to identify and Sky Walk 2 will tell you the name. Sky Walk 2 isn't the only app to offer such a facility, but in Sky Walk 2's case this feature is present in the free version of the app. Finding dark sky sites As Earth's population continues to grow, so does the problem of light pollution, so seeking out dark sky sites is essential for the best experience. (Image credit: Inigo Cia via Getty Images) It's a sad fact that light pollution has made it harder for astronomers to study the night sky. While the planets in our solar system are still visible, sky glow obscures more distant objects, such as fainter stars. You could travel to a dark sky reserve but, with the aid of one of several stargazing apps, it is also possible to find dark sky sites closer to home. Apps like Sky Safari and the simply named Light Pollution Map will show you the light pollution levels locally and globally, estimated on the Bortle scale. The latter app colors the map, with pink the most light pollution and black the least. In just a few seconds you can find out how light polluted your local area is, and use the map to find a location nearby where the sky is dark, or at least darker. Planning a stargazing trip Sky Safari 7 Pro is a stargazing app that will help you choose what you want to see and where. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) Are you planning a stargazing trip? Then you'll be happy to hear there's an app for that. There are several, in fact, but Sky Safari has all you need to plan your next outing. You can create observation lists, find out when and where objects are visible, and while it won't book your tickets for you, it comes close. Our reviewer Jamie Carter used the app to plan his observations of conjunctions, specific moon views and astrophotography opportunities. Coupled with its light pollution map, it will be a huge help in putting together an itinerary for your skywatching trip. Troubleshooting stargazing apps Hopefully you'll have a smooth experience, but if you're having issues, here are a few things to try. Take your phone out of its case. Magnetic clasps can interfere with internal sensors. Make sure location services are enabled . Many apps use GPS to show you the correct view. Check your phone's clock. If your clock is not set accurately, apps may display an incorrect sky Swoop your phone in a figure eight motion. This can help calibrate your phone's "compass". Make sure you have a signal, and that data is enabled. Unless the app has an offline mode you will still need a connection. Signal may be poor at dark sky sites. Check each app's permissions . Location aside, Augmented Reality (AR) stargazing apps will need camera access. We've got you covered with reviews and rankings of the best telescopes , binoculars , star projectors , cameras , drones , Lego , streaming and more.

item.title: Supermassive black hole blasts out a neon 'treble clef' | Space photo of the day for Oct. 16, 2026
item.description: null The "treble clef" galaxy cluster is an unusual source of radio waves, the Chandra X-ray observatory has found. (Image credit: X-ray: NASA/CXC/INAF-IRA/A. Botteon et al.; Infrared: UKIDSS-GPS ; Radio: ASTRON/LOFAR; Image processing: NASA/CXC/SAO/N. Wolk) What looks like a neon pink treble clef floating out in space is actually a bizarre source of radio waves spotted deep in the cosmos. What is it? Scientists using NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory have peered far out into space to look at strange radio waves coming from what they have nicknamed the "treble clef" because of its distinct shape, which looks a lot like the musical notation. Using Chandra, as well as the German Extended RÖntgen Survey with an Imaging Telescope Array ( eROSITA ) X-ray telescope, researchers looking at this strange sight spotted a big cloud of blue gas, which we can see in this image, along with radio signals (seen here in bright pink). They think that this object is actually a huge galaxy cluster made up of two different clusters that are in the process of merging. Why is it incredible? The researchers think they may have gotten to the bottom of where these radio waves are coming from, they report in a new study. The team thinks that the treble clef-shaped radio signals were created by an outburst from a supermassive black hole . They believe that this outburst pushed clouds of charged particles and magnetic fields away from the galaxy cluster's center, producing bright radio waves. According to the scientists, following this bright outburst, there was likely an extreme collision between two galaxy clusters. This cosmic smash-up either compressed or somehow reenergized these charged particles to amplify the radio signal. When we see beautiful images of objects in space such as this, they can seem just like peaceful, colorful, cosmic clouds. But when you look a bit deeper, these spectacular scenes can actually be evidence of violent, chaotic events. This work was described in a study published in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics.

item.title: He Wants AI Benchmarking To Be a Science, Not a Dark Art
item.description: Benchmarks are the rulers of AI, in both senses of the word. As measuring sticks, they work according to an extremely simple logic: If you want to know what an AI model can do, devise a standardized test to gauge it. But AI benchmarks can also dominate the behavior of the entire field. In 1987, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency’s first benchmark on automatic speech-to-text… Source
item.dc:creator: John Pavlus
item.content:encoded: Benchmarks are the rulers of AI, in both senses of the word. As measuring sticks, they work according to an extremely simple logic: If you want to know what an AI model can do, devise a standardized test to gauge it. But AI benchmarks can also dominate the behavior of the entire field. In 1987, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency’s first benchmark on automatic speech-to-text… Source

item.title: WIMBIZ Marks 25 Years of Global Impact, and Unveils Anniversary Logo
item.description: 2026 WIMBIZ Conference Communications Chair, Funmi Onuma; Member, WIMBIZ Board of Trustees, Rolake Akinkugbe-Filani; WIMBIZ 25th Anniversary Committee Chair, Awuneba Ajumogobia; Co-Founder, WIMBIZ, Morin Desalu; Co-Founder, WIMBIZ, Ifeyinwa Ighodalo; Co-Founder, WIMBIZ, Adeola Azeez; Member, WIMBIZ Board of Trustees, Osayi Alile; 2026 WIMBIZ Conference Planning Group Chair, Ronke Onadeko; Executive Director, WIMBIZ, Omowunmi Akingbohungbe; and 2026 WIMBIZ Conference Planning Group Vice Chair, Yemisi Peters, during the WIMBIZ@25 Press Conference in Lagos on Tuesday, October 13, 2026. Women in Management, Business and Public Service (WIMBIZ) has reaffirmed its commitment to advancing women’s leadership, strengthening women-led enterprises and expanding economic opportunities across Africa and globally as it celebrates 25 years of impact. The organisation made this commitment at a press conference held on Tuesday, 13 October 2026, at the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) Innovation Centre in Lagos, where it unveiled its 25th anniversary logo and highlighted the strategic priorities of its forthcoming 25TH Annual Conference. WIMBIZ announced Bennedikter China Molokwu , DF. CIoD, a corporate governance and strategy professional, as Chairperson of the WIMBIZ 25th Annual Conference. A past President of the Chartered Institute of Directors Nigeria, Molokwu has served on more than 15 boards and brings decades of experience in corporate governance, risk management and women’s empowerment to the annual conference. The press conference brought together founders, members of the Board of Trustees, the 25th Anniversary Committee, the 2026 Conference Planning Committee, media representatives, and partners, including IWOSAN and the Enterprise Development Centre (EDC). Reflecting on the organisation’s 25-year journey, Member, WIMBIZ Board of Trustees, Rolake Akinkugbe-Filani emphasised that while significant progress has been made, the pace of change must accelerate. She said, “Women are certainly on track, but the reality is that the world is not.” She highlighted that, despite decades of advocacy and progress, women remain underrepresented in management and political leadership, reinforcing the urgency of collective action to close the gender gap. WIMBIZ Board of Trustees member Osayi Alile reinforced the importance of collaboration in achieving this ambition, noting that advancing women’s leadership requires collective responsibility rather than isolated efforts. “Gender is not only nice to have. It is a strategic thing. It is an economic thing as well,” she emphasised, calling on stakeholders to recognise women’s participation as a critical driver of economic growth and sustainable development. WIMBIZ also called on the media to amplify the stories of women creating change, strengthen public awareness of gender inclusion and support the organisation’s efforts to expand opportunities for women in Nigeria, across Africa and globally. 2026 WIMBIZ Confer
